explanation.summary: Occupational hollow-bore needlestick from a known HIV-positive source with detectable viraemia is a high-risk exposure. ASHM recommends a 28-day three-drug regimen of tenofovir disoproxil-emtricitabine plus dolutegravir, started as soon as possible and always within 72 hours (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines).
key_points: PEP within 72 hours, ideally under 4 hours
Three-drug regimen mandatory for high-risk exposures
TDF-FTC + dolutegravir is first-line per ASHM
Baseline HIV, hepatitis B/C, renal function and pregnancy test required
explanation.pearls: Follow-up HIV serology at 6 and 12 weeks (fourth-generation assay); hepatitis B booster or immunoglobulin if not immune.

options.rationale: Zidovudine-lamivudine is a two-drug regimen from earlier ASHM guidance and is no longer first-line PEP because of inferior potency, resistance concerns and zidovudine's marrow and gastrointestinal toxicity. Current ASHM PEP guidelines mandate a three-drug regimen for all significant exposures (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines).

Efavirenz-based PEP is no longer preferred because of central nervous system side effects, teratogenicity concerns in the first trimester and lower tolerability, all of which reduce PEP completion rates. Integrase inhibitor-based regimens are now the standard third agent (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines).

Two-NRTI PEP is inadequate when the source is confirmed HIV-positive with detectable viraemia; adding an integrase inhibitor as the third drug is mandatory. Two-drug PEP is not endorsed for any exposure category in the current ASHM guidance (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines).

The ASHM National PEP Guidelines recommend a 28-day course of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate 300 mg plus emtricitabine 200 mg once daily combined with dolutegravir 50 mg once daily as first-line PEP after a significant occupational exposure to a known HIV-positive source with detectable viraemia. Commencement within 72 hours is essential, with the greatest efficacy inside four hours (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines).

PEP efficacy declines rapidly with delay and must be commenced within 72 hours, ideally within four hours of exposure. The source viral load is already known to be detectable and the exposure is high risk; deferring treatment risks failure of prophylaxis (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Primary PJP prophylaxis in HIV is triggered by CD4 count below 200 cells/microL (or oropharyngeal candidiasis or an AIDS-defining illness). Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is first-line and also covers toxoplasmosis at CD4 counts below 100 in IgG-positive patients (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).
key_points: PJP prophylaxis threshold: CD4 <200 cells/microL
Toxoplasma prophylaxis: CD4 <100 AND toxoplasma IgG positive
MAC prophylaxis: CD4 <50 (with azithromycin)
TMP-SMX 160/800 mg daily is first-line PJP prophylaxis
explanation.pearls: Prophylaxis can be stopped once CD4 rises above 200 for at least three months on suppressive ART.

options.rationale: Azithromycin prophylaxis is indicated for disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex when the CD4 count falls below 50 cells/microL. His CD4 of 148 is well above that threshold and does not warrant MAC prophylaxis (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

The ASHM HIV Management Guidelines and Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic recommend PJP primary prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole once the CD4 count falls below 200 cells/microL. His CD4 is 148 so prophylaxis is indicated. The same regimen also covers toxoplasmosis, which becomes relevant if CD4 falls below 100 and toxoplasma IgG is positive (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

Primary CMV prophylaxis is not routinely recommended in HIV even at very low CD4 counts because of toxicity, cost and lack of survival benefit. CMV disease is managed pre-emptively with retinal screening and treatment when disease is diagnosed, not with universal prophylaxis (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

Routine primary prophylaxis against cryptococcosis is not recommended in Australian practice; instead, cryptococcal antigen screening is offered when the CD4 count falls below 100 in high-prevalence settings, with pre-emptive fluconazole only if the antigen is positive (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

His CD4 count of 148 crosses the well-established PJP prophylaxis threshold of 200 cells/microL, so withholding prophylaxis exposes him to a preventable AIDS-defining pneumonia while awaiting immune reconstitution on antiretroviral therapy (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

explanation.summary: A detectable viral load after years of suppression is an adherence or absorption problem far more often than resistance. The first move is history: missed or late doses, a change in routine such as shift work, and any new medicine. Proton pump inhibitors, antacids, calcium, magnesium and iron chelate integrase inhibitors and markedly reduce absorption unless separation of dosing is observed. A repeat viral load confirms whether the result is real, and a resistance genotype is sent while the patient remains on therapy if viraemia persists above about 200 to 500 copies per millilitre. In context, low level blips happen and resolve, while sustained viraemia on a regimen the patient is actually taking is what defines virological failure and prompts a genotype-guided switch.
key_points: Adherence and absorption explain most rebound after long suppression.
Polyvalent cations and antacids reduce integrase inhibitor absorption.
Confirm with a repeat viral load before changing anything.
Send the genotype while the patient is still on therapy.
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about supplements and pharmacy purchases; patients often do not count calcium, iron or antacids as medicines when asked what they take.

options.rationale: Most rebound after long suppression is adherence or absorption, and polyvalent cations in supplements or antacids chelate integrase inhibitors; the history determines whether a repeat viral load and resistance genotype are next. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines; AMH)

A regimen change is appropriate once virological failure is confirmed on a repeat sample with a resistance genotype, or for intolerance, and switching blindly risks burning a future option. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines)

Adding a single agent to a failing regimen is functional monotherapy and selects resistance; additional agents are chosen from a genotype in multidrug-resistant disease. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines)
Treatment interruption is avoided because it allows viral rebound and immune decline, and genotyping needs viraemia on treatment to be informative. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines)

CD4 monitoring is for staging and prophylaxis decisions in advanced disease, and a six month wait allows resistance to accumulate on a partially active regimen. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines)

explanation.summary: In advanced HIV with CD4 below 50, disseminated MAC classically presents with fever, weight loss, anaemia and a cholestatic hepatitis picture. Mycobacterial blood cultures must be sent before empirical macrolide therapy because macrolide monotherapy of active disease drives resistance (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).
key_points: MAC prophylaxis threshold: CD4 <50 with azithromycin 1200 mg weekly
Rule out active disseminated MAC before commencing prophylaxis
Disseminated MAC treatment: clarithromycin (or azithromycin) plus ethambutol
Cholestatic ALP/GGT with wasting at low CD4 = think MAC
explanation.pearls: Prompt ART is still indicated; delaying ART for MAC treatment increases mortality more than IRIS risk.

options.rationale: Starting azithromycin prophylaxis before excluding active disseminated MAC risks selecting for macrolide resistance if occult MAC bacteraemia is present. Fever, wasting, anaemia and a cholestatic hepatitis picture at CD4 32 are highly suggestive of disseminated MAC, and blood mycobacterial cultures must be sent first (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

Cryptococcal antigen is negative, effectively excluding cryptococcal disease as the driver of his current presentation. Empirical fluconazole is not warranted and adds hepatotoxicity to an already deranged liver enzyme picture (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

QuantiFERON is negative, sputum smear is negative and there is no pulmonary infiltrate; empirical RIPE therapy is not indicated and would delay recognition of MAC. Antituberculous therapy also has significant interactions with antiretrovirals that require careful selection (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

CMV disease at CD4 below 50 typically causes retinitis, colitis or oesophagitis rather than a cholestatic hepatitis-and-wasting picture. Empirical valganciclovir carries substantial marrow toxicity and should not be initiated without evidence of end-organ CMV disease (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

At CD4 below 50 with fevers, wasting, anaemia and a cholestatic liver enzyme picture, disseminated MAC is the leading opportunistic infection. Mycobacterial blood cultures are the diagnostic test of choice and must be collected before empirical azithromycin because monotherapy of active disease drives macrolide resistance. Confirmed disseminated MAC is then treated with clarithromycin or azithromycin plus ethambutol, not with prophylactic monotherapy (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions in a toxoplasma-IgG-positive patient with CD4 below 100 are treated empirically for cerebral toxoplasmosis using sulfadiazine, pyrimethamine and folinic acid. Clinical and radiological response is assessed at 10 to 14 days; non-responders undergo biopsy for primary CNS lymphoma (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).
key_points: Toxoplasmosis risk: CD4 <100 with positive toxoplasma IgG
Empirical treatment before biopsy is standard for typical presentations
Sulfadiazine + pyrimethamine + folinic acid is first-line
Non-response by 14 days triggers biopsy for CNS lymphoma
explanation.pearls: TMP-SMX-based regimens provide both PJP and toxoplasmosis prophylaxis in CD4-below-100 patients with positive toxoplasma IgG.

options.rationale: Multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions in advanced HIV with CD4 below 100 and positive toxoplasma IgG have a pre-test probability of cerebral toxoplasmosis of over 80 per cent. ASHM and Therapeutic Guidelines recommend empirical sulfadiazine plus pyrimethamine plus folinic acid, with clinical and radiological reassessment at 10 to 14 days; failure to respond prompts biopsy to exclude primary CNS lymphoma (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

Biopsy is reserved for atypical presentations, toxoplasma IgG negative patients, single lesions with high suspicion for lymphoma on thallium SPECT or MRS, or failure of a 10 to 14 day empirical trial. In a typical multi-lesion IgG-positive presentation, empirical therapy is standard practice and biopsy is second-line (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

Amphotericin plus flucytosine is induction therapy for cryptococcal meningoencephalitis. Cryptococcal antigen is negative and imaging does not suggest cryptococcoma, making this empirical treatment inappropriate (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

Empirical corticosteroids can shrink CNS lymphoma temporarily and confound both imaging and biopsy interpretation. They should be avoided unless there is impending herniation from mass effect. Even then dexamethasone rather than methylprednisolone is preferred, and it is added to, not instead of, antimicrobial therapy (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

Primary CNS lymphoma typically presents as a single periventricular lesion in EBV-driven disease and requires histological confirmation before radiotherapy. Two lesions in a toxoplasma-IgG-positive patient favour toxoplasmosis; empirical radiotherapy without diagnosis is inappropriate (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

explanation.summary: ASHM 2024 preferred first-line antiretroviral therapy is an integrase inhibitor combined with two nucleoside/tide backbone drugs, most commonly bictegravir-tenofovir alafenamide-emtricitabine or dolutegravir-based combinations. These deliver rapid, durable viral suppression with a favourable side effect and interaction profile (Source: ASHM Antiretroviral Guidelines).
key_points: First-line: integrase inhibitor + 2 NRTI backbone
Bictegravir-TAF-FTC is a preferred single-tablet regimen
Efavirenz and boosted PIs are alternatives, not first-line
Long-acting injectables are switch options, not initiation
explanation.pearls: U=U: sustained undetectable viral load eliminates sexual transmission and supports safe conception planning.

options.rationale: Zidovudine-lamivudine-nevirapine is an obsolete first-line regimen with significant marrow, hepatic and hypersensitivity toxicity, and higher pill and dosing burden. It is no longer recommended by ASHM outside historic resource-limited contexts (Source: ASHM Antiretroviral Guidelines).

Efavirenz-based regimens are no longer preferred first-line in Australian guidance because of central nervous system adverse effects, historical first-trimester teratogenicity concerns and inferior tolerability compared with integrase inhibitor regimens. They are reserved as alternatives when preferred regimens are contraindicated (Source: ASHM Antiretroviral Guidelines).

Boosted protease inhibitor regimens are second-line in current ASHM guidance; they carry a higher pill burden, more drug interactions and a hyperbilirubinaemia signal, and are outperformed by integrase inhibitor regimens for tolerability and viral suppression rates (Source: ASHM Antiretroviral Guidelines).

ASHM 2024 preferred first-line antiretroviral regimens for treatment-naive adults are integrase strand transfer inhibitor based; bictegravir with tenofovir alafenamide and emtricitabine as a single-tablet regimen is a preferred option, with strong efficacy, low interaction profile, favourable pregnancy safety data (once conception occurs) and durable virological suppression suitable for a patient planning imminent conception (Source: ASHM Antiretroviral Guidelines).

Long-acting injectable cabotegravir with rilpivirine is approved as a switch option for patients already virologically suppressed on oral therapy, not for treatment initiation. It requires prior confirmed sensitivity and suppression, and is not appropriate as first-line initiation (Source: ASHM Antiretroviral Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Paradoxical tuberculosis-associated IRIS occurs when antiretroviral therapy is started in the setting of very low CD4 counts and pre-existing opportunistic infection, producing worsening clinical or radiographic features despite microbiological response. Management is to continue both therapies and add corticosteroids for moderate-to-severe cases, per the Meintjes trial and ASHM guidance (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).
key_points: IRIS risk highest with CD4 <100 and rapid viral load fall
Continue both antituberculous therapy and antiretroviral therapy
Exclude treatment failure and drug resistance first
Prednisolone 1.5 mg/kg daily for 2 weeks then taper (Meintjes trial)
explanation.pearls: Cryptococcal IRIS mandates delaying ART by 4-6 weeks after antifungal induction to reduce fatal CNS inflammation.

options.rationale: Interrupting antiretroviral therapy during paradoxical IRIS worsens outcomes by allowing HIV replication to rebound, delays immune recovery and does not resolve the inflammatory reaction; ASHM guidance is to continue both therapies wherever clinically feasible (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

Repeat susceptibility testing confirms ongoing drug sensitivity and there is no microbiological failure. The worsening clinical picture reflects immune reconstitution against persisting antigen, not treatment failure, so second-line antituberculous drugs are inappropriate (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

This is paradoxical tuberculosis-associated IRIS: worsening lymphadenopathy, fevers and radiographic disease within weeks of starting antiretroviral therapy at low CD4 count, with excluded treatment failure and no drug resistance. Both antituberculous therapy and antiretroviral therapy should continue, and moderate-to-severe symptomatic IRIS is treated with prednisolone approximately 1.5 mg/kg daily for two weeks followed by a taper, supported by the Meintjes randomised controlled trial and endorsed by ASHM (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

There is no clinical, radiographic or microbiological evidence of bacterial superinfection; he is haemodynamically stable, has no consolidation pattern of bacterial pneumonia and blood cultures are negative. Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics add toxicity without addressing the underlying inflammatory driver (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Excisional biopsy is not the first step in a patient with a confirmed tuberculosis diagnosis and typical timeline for paradoxical IRIS. Biopsy is reserved for atypical presentations or diagnostic uncertainty regarding lymphoma or a resistant organism, neither of which applies here (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

explanation.summary: PrEP is indicated for high-risk sexual exposure and requires baseline HIV, renal function and hepatitis serology before initiation. A recent exposure inside or just outside the 72-hour PEP window requires acute HIV exclusion before starting a two-drug PrEP regimen, because starting PrEP during unrecognised acute HIV selects for resistance (Source: ASHM PrEP Guidelines).
key_points: PrEP: TDF-FTC daily or event-driven 2-1-1 for MSM
Baseline: HIV Ag/Ab (+/- RNA), renal function, hepatitis B/C, STIs
Exclude acute HIV before starting to avoid resistance
Three-monthly HIV, renal function and STI monitoring on PrEP
explanation.pearls: PEP window is 72 hours from exposure; beyond that, focus shifts to acute HIV exclusion and bridging to PrEP.

options.rationale: The condom failure four days ago is outside the 72-hour PEP window, so PEP cannot be started for that exposure; instead, the priority is to exclude occult acute HIV before commencing PrEP. Given his high-risk profile and imminent PrEP eligibility, ASHM guidance is to defer daily PrEP until acute HIV is excluded with a fourth-generation antigen-antibody test plus HIV RNA at follow-up, then commence tenofovir disoproxil-emtricitabine PrEP with three-monthly HIV, renal function and STI monitoring. In this scenario, restarting the described sequence with PEP first is not appropriate given the timing; the safest actionable pathway is to bridge to PrEP after HIV exclusion (Source: ASHM PrEP Guidelines).

Starting standard daily PrEP without addressing the condom failure four days ago risks converting an unrecognised acute HIV infection into a PrEP-induced integrase or NRTI resistance selection scenario, because a two-drug regimen is inadequate to suppress established infection. The exposure four days ago is within the 72-hour PEP window boundary and must be evaluated first (Source: ASHM PrEP Guidelines).

Sending baseline HIV RNA plus fourth-generation testing is appropriate, but this option omits the crucial actionable component of scheduling explicit PrEP commencement once results confirm HIV-negative status, and does not address the ongoing high-risk behaviour in the interim. It is a diagnostic step rather than a management plan (Source: ASHM PrEP Guidelines).

Methamphetamine use in sexual contexts is a marker of higher HIV acquisition risk and an indication for PrEP rather than a contraindication. Withholding PrEP because of substance use is not supported by ASHM guidance and reinforces stigma (Source: ASHM PrEP Guidelines).

Event-driven 2-1-1 dosing is only supported for men who have sex with men where sexual events are predictable, and still requires baseline HIV, renal and hepatitis testing to exclude acute HIV and renal impairment before commencement. Skipping baseline HIV testing risks PrEP-induced resistance if occult acute HIV is present (Source: ASHM PrEP Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Uncomplicated cystitis in non-pregnant women with normal renal function is treated empirically with a short course of trimethoprim (3 days) or nitrofurantoin (5 days) per eTG. Culture is not required for a first uncomplicated episode with a classic presentation. Cefalexin and beta-lactams are second-line or reserved for pregnancy. Fluoroquinolones are avoided outside complicated infections.
key_points: Trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 3 days OR nitrofurantoin 100 mg 6-hourly for 5 days are eTG first-line.
Amoxicillin is inadequate empirically due to E. coli resistance in Australia.
Fluoroquinolones are reserved for complicated or resistant infection.
Nitrofurantoin duration is 5 days, not 3 - a common prescribing error.
explanation.pearls: Nitrofurantoin needs eGFR above 45 mL/min/1.73m^2 to concentrate in urine adequately; below that, switch to trimethoprim or cefalexin.

sources.label: RACGP - Urinary tract infection in adults

options.rationale: Amoxicillin monotherapy is not recommended empirically for uncomplicated cystitis in Australia because of high E. coli resistance rates. It is only appropriate when susceptibility is confirmed on culture (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook - Amoxicillin).

Cefalexin is an eTG alternative when first-line agents are unsuitable, not the primary choice for uncomplicated cystitis. It has broader ecological impact and is preferred in pregnancy rather than in non-pregnant women with normal renal function (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute cystitis).

eTG lists trimethoprim 300 mg orally, daily for 3 days as a first-line option for acute cystitis in non-pregnant women with normal renal function, alongside nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally 6-hourly for 5 days. Either agent is acceptable first-line; local resistance patterns and tolerability guide the choice (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute cystitis).

Fluoroquinolones are reserved for complicated infections or resistant organisms in Australia and are not first-line for uncomplicated cystitis because of collateral resistance and tendinopathy or QT risk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute cystitis).

Nitrofurantoin is a first-line agent but the eTG duration for acute uncomplicated cystitis is 5 days, not 3. A 3-day course underdoses the regimen and risks early recurrence (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute cystitis).

explanation.summary: eTG stratifies pyelonephritis by severity. Non-severe cases who tolerate oral fluids and are haemodynamically stable receive a single IV gentamicin loading dose plus early oral step-down (trimethoprim, amoxicillin-clavulanate, or cefalexin depending on culture) for a total 10-14 days. Severe sepsis, pregnancy, obstruction or failed oral therapy triggers full IV therapy and admission.
key_points: Single-dose gentamicin plus oral step-down is the eTG default for non-severe pyelonephritis.
Nitrofurantoin is contraindicated - inadequate tissue penetration.
Oral cefalexin monotherapy is not recommended for pyelonephritis.
Total course is 10-14 days, longer than cystitis.
explanation.pearls: Gentamicin dosing uses ideal body weight (or dose-adjusted weight if BMI over 30) at 4-7 mg/kg; a single loading dose rarely requires level monitoring.

options.rationale: Dual IV therapy is unnecessary when she is haemodynamically stable, tolerating oral fluids and without sepsis criteria. eTG reserves combination IV beta-lactam plus aminoglycoside for severe sepsis, septic shock or failed initial therapy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute pyelonephritis).

eTG recommends a single loading dose of IV gentamicin (4 to 7 mg/kg IBW) followed by oral step-down for non-severe pyelonephritis in patients able to tolerate oral therapy. Trimethoprim 300 mg daily for a total 10-14 day course is a listed oral option pending susceptibilities (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute pyelonephritis).

Nitrofurantoin does not achieve adequate tissue concentrations in renal parenchyma and is contraindicated in pyelonephritis. Its use is restricted to lower urinary tract infection (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook - Nitrofurantoin).

Oral cefalexin has inadequate serum concentrations for empirical pyelonephritis therapy and is not an eTG first-line option. Cefalexin is reserved for cystitis in pregnancy, not pyelonephritis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute pyelonephritis).

Oral ciprofloxacin is an eTG alternative when aminoglycosides are contraindicated, but is not first-line given Australian E. coli fluoroquinolone resistance and adverse effect profile. Reserve for confirmed susceptibility or beta-lactam contraindication (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute pyelonephritis).

explanation.summary: Catheter-associated bacteriuria is almost universal after several days of catheterisation, but is not itself an indication for treatment. eTG and IDSA guidance treat only symptomatic CAUTI, defined by new fever, suprapubic or flank pain, delirium in older adults, rigors, or clinical sepsis. Antibiotics for asymptomatic bacteriuria drive resistance and C. difficile without benefit. Exceptions are pregnancy and immediately before urological procedures with mucosal trauma.
key_points: Do not routinely culture catheter urine in asymptomatic patients.
Treat only symptomatic CAUTI (fever, suprapubic or flank pain, delirium, sepsis).
Remove or replace long-standing catheters when symptomatic CAUTI is diagnosed.
Pregnancy and pre-urological procedure are the only asymptomatic exceptions.
explanation.pearls: New unexplained delirium in an older catheterised patient with no other localising features is not enough to diagnose CAUTI - look for a second sign (fever, pain, rigors) before starting antibiotics.

options.rationale: Treating asymptomatic catheter-associated bacteriuria promotes resistance and Clostridioides difficile infection without altering outcomes. eTG explicitly recommends against antibiotic treatment in this scenario (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Catheter-associated UTI).

Any antibiotic prescription for asymptomatic catheter bacteriuria is inappropriate. Choice of agent does not change the recommendation - no treatment is indicated (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Catheter-associated UTI).

Neither empirical antibiotics nor routine catheter change is indicated for asymptomatic bacteriuria. Catheter change without symptoms simply reseeds the bladder with new organisms (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Catheter-associated UTI).

Asymptomatic catheter-associated bacteriuria in a patient without local or systemic symptoms should not be treated with antibiotics. Repeat culture is also not indicated and simply generates more positive results. Proceed with catheter removal as planned (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Catheter-associated UTI).

Blood cultures and IV antibiotics are reserved for suspected sepsis or systemic infection. He has no fever, tachycardia, hypotension, delirium or raised inflammatory markers (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Catheter-associated UTI).

explanation.summary: UTI in pregnancy requires prompt treatment because it increases risk of preterm labour, low birth weight and pyelonephritis. Cefalexin is the safe default across all gestations. Nitrofurantoin is acceptable in first and second trimesters but avoided at or near term (from about 38 weeks) due to neonatal G6PD-related haemolysis risk. Trimethoprim is avoided in the first trimester (folate antagonist) and generally when alternatives exist. Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is also treated because of pyelonephritis and preterm birth risk.
key_points: Cefalexin 500 mg 12-hourly for 5 days is the eTG default in pregnancy.
Nitrofurantoin: avoid at term (from 38 weeks) and during labour.
Trimethoprim: avoid in first trimester (folate antagonist).
Fluoroquinolones are contraindicated in pregnancy.
Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy - unlike non-pregnant adults.
explanation.pearls: In a woman at 38+ weeks with UTI, choose cefalexin first line - nitrofurantoin should be off the mental menu because delivery may occur during the course and the neonate is unshielded by placental folate metabolism.

Australian Medicines Handbook - Trimethoprim in pregnancy

options.rationale: Cefalexin is the eTG-preferred oral empirical agent for cystitis in pregnancy at any gestation because it is safe throughout pregnancy and has predictable coverage of common uropathogens. A 5-day course is standard (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - UTI in pregnancy).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - UTI in pregnancy

options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin is avoided at or near term (from 38 weeks and during labour) because of the neonatal haemolytic anaemia risk if the neonate has G6PD deficiency. It is otherwise acceptable earlier in pregnancy (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook - Nitrofurantoin in pregnancy).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook - Nitrofurantoin in pregnancy

options.rationale: Trimethoprim is a folate antagonist and is avoided particularly in the first trimester (neural tube defect risk) and generally throughout pregnancy when alternatives exist. Cefalexin is preferred (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook - Trimethoprim in pregnancy).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook - Trimethoprim in pregnancy

options.rationale: Amoxicillin monotherapy is inadequate empirically in Australia because of high E. coli resistance; it can be used only when susceptibility is confirmed on culture (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - UTI in pregnancy).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - UTI in pregnancy

options.rationale: Fluoroquinolones are contraindicated in pregnancy because of fetal cartilage toxicity concerns and are not empirical options for UTI in pregnancy at any gestation (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook - Fluoroquinolones in pregnancy).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook - Fluoroquinolones in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Recurrent UTI is defined as two episodes in 6 months or three in 12 months. Workup includes urinary tract imaging and PVR, with cystoscopy considered by urology for atypical features. Once complicating pathology is excluded, behavioural measures come first (hydration, post-coital voiding, avoiding spermicides). If insufficient, options are post-coital, patient-initiated stand-by, or continuous nightly prophylaxis for 6 months. Topical vaginal oestrogen is a strong option in post-menopausal women.
key_points: Recurrent UTI threshold: 2 in 6 months or 3 in 12 months.
Nitrofurantoin 50 mg nocte OR trimethoprim 150 mg nocte for 6 months.
Post-coital prophylaxis when temporally linked to intercourse.
Vaginal oestrogen for post-menopausal women reduces recurrence.
explanation.pearls: Vaginal oestrogen (estriol cream twice weekly) reduces UTI recurrence in post-menopausal women by roughly half - consider adding it in this patient given surgical menopause at 40.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Recurrent UTI in women

options.rationale: eTG recommends continuous antibiotic prophylaxis with nitrofurantoin 50 mg nocte (alternative trimethoprim 150 mg nocte) for 6 months in women with two or more UTIs in 6 months, or three or more in 12 months, unresponsive to behavioural measures. Structural workup has excluded a treatable cause (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Recurrent UTI in women).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Recurrent UTI in women

options.rationale: Post-coital prophylaxis is an option when UTIs are temporally linked to intercourse. Her history does not identify a coital trigger and she is post-menopausal following oophorectomy, so continuous prophylaxis is more appropriate (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Recurrent UTI in women).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Recurrent UTI in women

options.rationale: Patient-initiated stand-by therapy is reasonable for women who reliably recognise symptoms and prefer to avoid daily antibiotics. It does not prevent recurrence and is a step below continuous prophylaxis when frequency meets threshold (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Recurrent UTI in women).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Recurrent UTI in women

options.rationale: Advanced imaging is reserved for complicated recurrent UTI, suspected upper tract disease, non-E. coli organisms, or persistent haematuria. She has a normal ultrasound and cystoscopy, and CT would add ionising radiation without expected yield (Source: RACGP - Recurrent UTI in women).

Cranberry products have inconsistent evidence and are not recommended by eTG or RACGP as a substitute for antibiotic prophylaxis when threshold criteria are met. May be a patient adjunct but not the primary answer (Source: RACGP - Recurrent UTI in women).

explanation.summary: All UTIs in men are considered complicated and require a full workup and a longer course than uncomplicated female cystitis. Acute bacterial prostatitis presents with dysuria, pelvic or perineal pain and an exquisitely tender prostate on DRE (avoid vigorous prostate massage - bacteraemia risk). Empirical eTG therapy is trimethoprim 300 mg daily, cotrimoxazole 160/800 mg 12-hourly, or ciprofloxacin 500 mg 12-hourly, all for 14 days pending culture. Severe features (sepsis, urinary retention) prompt IV therapy and admission.
key_points: All UTIs in men are complicated - always culture, always longer course.
Trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 14 days is first-line for acute prostatitis.
Avoid nitrofurantoin, cefalexin, amoxicillin - poor prostatic penetration.
Avoid vigorous DRE prostate massage in acute prostatitis - bacteraemia risk.
explanation.pearls: Chronic bacterial prostatitis (recurrent UTI in a man with the same organism) usually needs 4-6 weeks of ciprofloxacin, reflecting sustained deep prostatic clearance.

options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin does not penetrate prostatic tissue and is not effective for acute bacterial prostatitis. It is restricted to lower urinary tract infection in women (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook - Nitrofurantoin).

A 5-day course is the duration for uncomplicated cystitis, not acute prostatitis. Undertreated prostatitis can progress to abscess or chronic bacterial prostatitis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute prostatitis).
Cefalexin has poor prostatic penetration and inadequate coverage for acute prostatitis. It is not an eTG option for this indication (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute prostatitis).

Beta-lactams have poor prostatic penetration and are not first-line for acute prostatitis. eTG prefers trimethoprim, cotrimoxazole or ciprofloxacin (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute prostatitis).

Acute bacterial prostatitis needs an agent with prostatic penetration and a prolonged course. eTG recommends trimethoprim 300 mg orally daily for 14 days (alternative sulfamethoxazole plus trimethoprim or ciprofloxacin) as first-line empirical therapy in men without severe features (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute prostatitis).

explanation.summary: An obstructed infected upper urinary tract - most commonly caused by a retained stone or blocked stent - is a surgical emergency. Antibiotics alone cannot penetrate an obstructed collecting system; decompression by percutaneous nephrostomy (interventional radiology) or ureteric stent exchange (urology) is the definitive intervention and must occur within hours. Source control failure is the most common reason for progression to septic shock and death in urosepsis. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign lists source control as one of the hour-1 bundle priorities.
key_points: Obstructed infected kidney = surgical emergency: source control within hours.
Percutaneous nephrostomy or retrograde stent exchange are both acceptable.
Antibiotics do not penetrate an obstructed system.
Hydrocortisone is an adjunct for refractory shock, not initial therapy.
Retained stents can become nidus for encrustation and obstruction over weeks.
explanation.pearls: Any ureteric stent left beyond its labelled dwell time (commonly 3 to 12 months) is a source-control failure waiting to happen; document stent removal or exchange dates in the discharge summary.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Sepsis and septic shock
Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand - Obstructed infected kidney

options.rationale: Broadening antibiotic spectrum without source control will not reverse septic shock driven by an obstructed infected upper tract. Vancomycin is not indicated for typical urosepsis unless MRSA is suspected (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Sepsis and septic shock).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Sepsis and septic shock

options.rationale: Obstructed infected upper urinary tract is a surgical emergency and source control - percutaneous nephrostomy or retrograde stent exchange - is time-critical and must not be delayed for imaging or antibiotic re-dosing. Antibiotics alone will not resolve pyonephrosis (Source: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand - Obstructed infected kidney; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021).
source_refs: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand - Obstructed infected kidney

options.rationale: The obstruction is already demonstrated on bedside ultrasound and a contrast CT will delay definitive source control by hours in a patient with vasopressor-requiring septic shock and worsening kidney function. Non-contrast CT may be arranged en route to intervention if genuinely required (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021).

Hydrocortisone is a Surviving Sepsis adjunct only after adequate fluids and vasopressors have failed to restore perfusion, and never replaces source control. It is not the priority in obstructed pyonephrosis (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021).

A urethral catheter measures bladder output but does not decompress an obstructed upper tract above a retained ureteric stent. Delaying source control by an hour in vasopressor-requiring urosepsis worsens outcome (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021).

explanation.summary: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is normally not treated because it does not improve outcomes and drives resistance. The two accepted exceptions are pregnancy (risk of pyelonephritis and preterm labour) and before a urological procedure that breaches mucosa (TURP, ureteroscopy, prostate biopsy). In both scenarios, targeted therapy based on the identified organism replaces empirical prophylaxis. For TURP, IV targeted therapy at induction plus a short peri-operative course is the eTG and IDSA-endorsed approach.
key_points: Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria only in: pregnancy or before urological mucosal-breach procedures.
Target therapy to the identified organism, not generic prophylaxis.
Standard cefazolin skin prophylaxis alone is inadequate when a known uropathogen exists.
Prostate biopsy prophylaxis is separately covered by eTG - targeted to prior rectal swab organisms.
Vancomycin is reserved for VRE or true beta-lactam allergy.
explanation.pearls: For trans-rectal prostate biopsy, current AU practice is a peri-procedural augmented regimen guided by pre-procedure rectal swab or targeted culture (given rising fluoroquinolone resistance in E. coli) - not routine ciprofloxacin monotherapy.

sources.label: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Standard skin-flora surgical prophylaxis is inadequate when a resistant or specifically identified uropathogen is known to be present pre-operatively. Manipulation of infected urothelium risks bacteraemia and sepsis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Surgical prophylaxis; Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand).

Indefinite deferral is not required. Treatment targeted to the identified organism starting shortly before the procedure is sufficient; sterilisation of urine over multiple cultures is not the standard (Source: IDSA - Asymptomatic Bacteriuria (2019)).

A single oral dose does not provide reliable peri-operative tissue and urine concentrations and does not treat the underlying bacteriuria. IV targeted therapy starting shortly before the procedure is preferred (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Surgical prophylaxis).

Asymptomatic bacteriuria should NOT normally be treated - the two exceptions are pregnancy and before a urological procedure with mucosal trauma (such as TURP). eTG and IDSA recommend targeted therapy based on the identified organism starting shortly before the procedure, with continuation only for the peri-operative period (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Surgical prophylaxis; IDSA - Asymptomatic Bacteriuria (2019)).

Vancomycin is reserved for vancomycin-resistant enterococcus or beta-lactam allergy. This isolate is amoxicillin-susceptible and vancomycin adds nothing but ecological cost and nephrotoxicity risk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Surgical prophylaxis).

explanation.summary: Warfarin reversal strategy is tiered by INR and bleeding. INR 4.5 to 10 without bleeding: withhold warfarin, consider oral vitamin K 1 to 2 mg if additional risk. INR over 10 without bleeding: withhold warfarin, oral vitamin K 3 to 5 mg. Any major bleed at any INR: PCC 25 to 50 IU per kg plus IV vitamin K 5 to 10 mg. Mechanical valves require avoidance of over-reversal because sub-therapeutic INR is a stroke risk.
key_points: INR over 8 no bleeding: withhold warfarin plus oral vitamin K 1 to 2 mg
Major bleeding at any INR: PCC 25 to 50 IU per kg IV plus IV vitamin K
Avoid IV vitamin K 10 mg in mechanical valve unless bleeding - risk of over-reversal
Clarithromycin (and other macrolides) is a well-known warfarin interaction
explanation.pearls: Small oral vitamin K (1 to 2 mg) works within 24 hours without making warfarin resistant, whereas a 10 mg IV dose can leave a mechanical valve unprotected.

options.rationale: At INR over 8 without bleeding, oral vitamin K reduces bleeding risk more reliably than withholding alone, without creating warfarin resistance if the dose is kept low (1 to 2 mg). Withholding alone is used for INR 5 to 8 without bleeding. (Source: eTG complete: Warfarin reversal)

For INR over 8 without bleeding, the AMH/eTG recommendation is to withhold warfarin and give low-dose oral vitamin K (1 to 2 mg) to bring INR into range within 24 hours without causing warfarin resistance. Higher doses (5 mg or more) or IV vitamin K risk over-reversal and make re-anticoagulation difficult, particularly important in mechanical valves. (Source: eTG complete: Warfarin reversal)

PCC is reserved for major bleeding or urgent surgical need, not asymptomatic supra-therapeutic INR. It carries thromboembolic risk which is particularly relevant in a mechanical valve. (Source: eTG complete: Warfarin reversal)

IV vitamin K at 10 mg over-reverses the anticoagulation and leaves the mechanical valve unprotected; it also creates warfarin resistance for days. Reserved for major bleeding. (Source: eTG complete: Warfarin reversal)

FFP is not indicated for asymptomatic supra-therapeutic INR; it carries transfusion risks and takes hours to correct INR. Reserved for major bleeding when PCC is unavailable. (Source: eTG complete: Warfarin reversal)

explanation.summary: Acute type B aortic dissection is managed medically with rigorous impulse control - HR under 60 and SBP 100 to 120 mmHg - to reduce dP/dt and shear stress on the false lumen. Beta blockade goes first (esmolol infusion or labetalol) and vasodilator (nitroprusside or GTN) is added after rate control to avoid reflex tachycardia. TEVAR is reserved for complicated dissection.
key_points: Type B uncomplicated: medical impulse control HR under 60 and SBP 100 to 120
Beta blocker before vasodilator to avoid reflex tachycardia and increased dP/dt
TEVAR for complicated type B: rupture, malperfusion, refractory pain or BP, expansion
Type A always for surgery
explanation.pearls: The core physiology in dissection BP control is dP/dt - starting a vasodilator without a beta blocker raises shear stress even as BP drops.

options.rationale: A single 5 mg IV bolus of metoprolol will not achieve sustained impulse control; ongoing infusion of esmolol or labetalol is required. Systolic under 140 is too permissive - the target is 100 to 120 mmHg. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

GTN monotherapy causes reflex tachycardia and increases dP/dt; heart rate under 100 is too permissive and misses the impulse control target that is the core physiological rationale. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

Sublingual nifedipine has unpredictable BP effect and no rate control; BP under 100 systolic risks under-perfusion of dissection branch vessels. Not a first-line agent in aortic dissection. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

Uncomplicated type B dissection is managed medically; TEVAR is reserved for complicated type B (rupture, malperfusion, refractory pain, refractory hypertension despite maximal medical therapy, false lumen expansion). Bypassing medical therapy exposes to procedural risk without indication. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

Acute type B dissection is managed medically with impulse control - heart rate under 60 and systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg to reduce dP/dt (rate of pressure rise). Beta blockade is given first (esmolol or labetalol) to blunt the reflex tachycardia from vasodilators; nitroprusside or GTN is added second for residual BP. Starting with pure vasodilator alone causes reflex tachycardia and worsens shear stress. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

explanation.summary: Trauma major haemorrhage triggers MTP - 1:1:1 red cells : FFP : platelets with early cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen under 1.5, TXA 1 g IV within 3 hours (repeat at 8 h), and IV calcium for citrate-related hypocalcaemia. Isolated red cell transfusion creates dilutional coagulopathy; VIIa is a last-resort agent, not a first choice.
key_points: MTP triggers: ABC score, shock index over 1, ongoing haemorrhage, coagulopathy
Balanced ratio 1:1:1 red cells : FFP : platelets
Cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen under 1.5 g/L; TXA within 3 h
IV calcium for citrate-induced hypocalcaemia during large transfusion
explanation.pearls: Hypocalcaemia from citrate is under-recognised in massive transfusion - give calcium empirically after 4 units of blood or if ionised calcium is under 1.1.

sources.label: CRASH-2 trial for TXA in trauma

options.rationale: In active haemorrhage MTP uses empiric 1:1:1 including platelets; waiting for the count to drop below 50 accepts avoidable dilutional coagulopathy and worsens outcome. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Protocol template)

Isolated red cell transfusion without FFP, platelets and cryoprecipitate creates a dilutional coagulopathy on top of the trauma-induced coagulopathy. The 1:1:1 ratio is the AU standard for major haemorrhage in trauma. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Protocol template)

PCC is reserved for warfarin reversal or bleeding on DOAC (specific to factor Xa inhibitor bleeding); it is not standard in trauma-induced coagulopathy where FFP and cryoprecipitate are preferred and target multiple factor deficiencies. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Protocol template)

He meets ABC score and shock-index criteria for MTP activation: ongoing haemorrhage, shock, coagulopathy (INR 1.8, low fibrinogen, thrombocytopenia), acidosis and hypocalcaemia. NBA guideline for MTP is 1:1:1 red cells : FFP : platelets, with early cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen under 1.5, TXA within 3 hours of injury, and IV calcium for hypocalcaemia from citrate. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Protocol template)

Recombinant VIIa is a last-resort agent with thromboembolic risk; it is not first-line and never a substitute for balanced blood product resuscitation. NBA guidance restricts it to specialist decision. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Protocol template)

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection kills through delay - the surgical debridement window is 6 hours. Clues that shift the diagnosis from cellulitis are pain-out-of-proportion, tenderness beyond erythema, dusky skin, sensory loss (nerve necrosis), high LRINEC, and fascial gas or fluid on imaging. Empirical antibiotics per eTG are meropenem plus clindamycin plus vancomycin.
key_points: Pain out of proportion, sensory loss, and dusky skin are the necrotising red flags
LRINEC 6 or more is intermediate risk; 8 or more is high risk
Surgical debridement within 6 hours is the mortality lever, not the antibiotic
AU empirical regimen: meropenem plus clindamycin plus vancomycin
explanation.pearls: The LRINEC score misses about a third of confirmed cases - if the clinical picture screams necrotising, do not let a low score reassure you.

sources.label: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections

options.rationale: Flucloxacillin monotherapy under-covers gram-negative and anaerobic organisms in necrotising fasciitis; waiting 4 hours delays the required surgical control that dominates mortality reduction. Cellulitis is not the diagnosis here. (Source: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections

options.rationale: Necrotising fasciitis requires urgent surgical debridement within 6 hours - the pain-out-of-proportion, dusky skin, reduced sensation (nerve necrosis), high LRINEC score, and fascial gas on ultrasound are all supportive. Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics per eTG include meropenem plus clindamycin (for exotoxin suppression) plus vancomycin (for MRSA cover). Antibiotics do not substitute for surgical control. (Source: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections

options.rationale: MRI delays surgery in a time-critical infection where clinical and bedside imaging findings are already diagnostic; every hour of delay increases mortality. Ceftriaxone plus metronidazole is not the AU empirical regimen for necrotising fasciitis. (Source: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections

options.rationale: Hyperbaric oxygen is an adjunct after surgical debridement and antibiotics have been initiated; it is not the first-line intervention and is not universally recommended. Delay for HBO would be catastrophic. (Source: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections

options.rationale: Bedside I and D does not achieve the wide operative debridement required and may worsen sepsis by opening the plane without full source control. Definitive theatre-based debridement is mandatory. (Source: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections

explanation.summary: Type A aortic dissection involves the ascending aorta and is a surgical emergency because of proximal extension into pericardium, coronaries and aortic valve. Untreated mortality is 1 percent per hour; open surgical repair is life-saving. Perioperative medical management still targets HR under 60 and SBP 100 to 120 mmHg via beta blockade first. Type B (descending only) is managed medically unless complicated.
key_points: Stanford type A: involves ascending aorta - open surgical repair
Stanford type B: descending only - medical impulse control, TEVAR if complicated
Medical impulse control still applies pre-op for both: HR under 60, SBP 100 to 120
Antiplatelets and pericardiocentesis are contraindicated in a dissecting aorta
explanation.pearls: Even in type A the pre-theatre plan is beta blockade first - vasodilator alone would raise dP/dt and worsen the tear before the surgeon arrives.

options.rationale: Involvement of the ascending aorta (Stanford type A) is a surgical emergency because of risk of proximal extension into pericardium (tamponade), coronary arteries (MI) and aortic regurgitation. Perioperative medical management still requires impulse control - HR under 60 and SBP 100 to 120 mmHg via beta blockade first. Delaying for medical management alone is not sufficient for type A. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

Medical management alone is the strategy for uncomplicated type B (descending), not for type A (ascending). Type A has 1 percent per hour mortality without surgery. Delaying repair for medical control alone would be fatal. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

TEVAR is used for descending aortic dissection (type B) with complications. It cannot address the ascending aorta or the root without special hybrid procedures; open surgical repair is the standard for type A. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

There is no tamponade physiology so pericardiocentesis is not indicated; pericardiocentesis in a dissecting aorta can worsen bleeding into the pericardium by relieving tamponade. Nitrate infusion without beta blockade would worsen dP/dt. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

Antiplatelet loading is contraindicated in aortic dissection - it increases bleeding risk into the false lumen and pericardium. Troponin is not elevated and imaging shows a dissection, not ACS. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

explanation.summary: AU sepsis management uses the one-hour bundle: obtain cultures without delaying antibiotics past 45 min, give broad-spectrum antibiotics matched to source, measure lactate, start 30 mL per kg crystalloid, and add noradrenaline if MAP under 65 after fluid. For catheter-associated urinary sepsis with shock, eTG recommends piperacillin-tazobactam plus gentamicin (single-dose aminoglycoside to cover Pseudomonas and gram-negatives). Source control includes catheter change.
key_points: One-hour bundle: cultures, lactate, antibiotics, fluid 30 mL per kg, vasopressor if MAP under 65 after fluid
Do not delay antibiotics for cultures past 45 min - each hour of delay increases mortality
Catheter-associated urosepsis with shock: piperacillin-tazobactam plus single-dose gentamicin
Source control (catheter change) is part of care, not optional
explanation.pearls: Antibiotic timing dominates mortality in septic shock - the target is under 45 minutes for the first dose.

sources.label: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock

options.rationale: Antibiotic delay in septic shock is associated with increased mortality (up to 7 percent per hour). Cultures should not gate antibiotic timing - obtain cultures but give antibiotics within an hour of recognition. (Source: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock)
source_refs: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock

options.rationale: The Surviving Sepsis one-hour bundle applied in AU practice: obtain cultures before antibiotics (do not delay antibiotics more than 45 min), broad-spectrum antibiotics targeted to source (piperacillin-tazobactam plus gentamicin for urinary sepsis with sepsis physiology per eTG), 30 mL per kg crystalloid, lactate measurement, and noradrenaline if MAP under 65 after fluid resuscitation. Source control via catheter change is part of care. (Source: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock)
source_refs: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock

options.rationale: Ceftriaxone plus metronidazole under-covers Pseudomonas and enterococci in a catheter-associated urinary sepsis from a nursing home; oral metronidazole in a hypotensive patient is unpredictable in absorption. Fluid volume of 500 mL is insufficient; 30 mL per kg (about 1.8 L for 60 kg) is the initial target. (Source: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock)
source_refs: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock

options.rationale: Vasopressor before adequate fluid resuscitation is generally inappropriate; noradrenaline is added when MAP remains under 65 after fluid resuscitation. Skipping cultures forfeits pathogen data used to narrow therapy. (Source: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock)
source_refs: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock

options.rationale: Antibiotic monotherapy without fluid resuscitation and cultures loses the physiological rescue components of the bundle. The AU one-hour bundle demands cultures, lactate, fluids, antibiotics, and vasopressor as a coordinated set. (Source: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock)
source_refs: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock

explanation.summary: Sub-acute LV free wall rupture is the leading post-MI mechanical complication at day 3 to 7 in a patient with a completed transmural infarct. It presents with sudden cardiovascular collapse and tamponade physiology (JVP elevation with absent y-descent, hypotension, RV diastolic collapse), often with a falling haemoglobin as blood accumulates in the pericardium. Definitive treatment is emergency surgical repair; pericardiocentesis is a bridge only, and DAPT amplifies bleeding risk.
key_points: Free wall rupture typically day 3 to 7 post-MI; peaks in transmural infarcts
Tamponade physiology plus falling Hb without external bleeding is the fingerprint
Emergency surgical repair is definitive; pericardiocentesis is temporising
Dressler syndrome is weeks later and rarely causes tamponade
explanation.pearls: A falling Hb into a growing pericardial effusion at day 6 post-MI is the free wall rupture story - pericardiocentesis alone lets the tamponade lose its haemostatic role.

options.rationale: Recurrent stent thrombosis presents with new ST elevation and rising troponin; her troponin is on downtrend and ECG shows no new ST shift. The tamponade physiology and falling Hb identify a mechanical complication rather than acute reinfarction. (Source: eTG complete: Post-MI mechanical complications)

Dressler syndrome typically occurs 2 to 6 weeks post-MI with pleuritic chest pain, low-grade fever, small pericardial effusion without tamponade, and inflammatory markers up. This patient has tamponade physiology, falling Hb and is 6 days post-MI, which fits free wall rupture rather than post-cardiac injury pericarditis. (Source: eTG complete: Post-MI mechanical complications)

Post-MI VSD produces a new pan-systolic murmur with left-to-right shunt on echo colour flow, not a pericardial effusion with tamponade. Falling Hb into the pericardial space is not the VSD pattern. (Source: eTG complete: Post-MI mechanical complications)

Papillary muscle rupture causes acute severe mitral regurgitation with pulmonary oedema and a new murmur but not typically a large pericardial effusion. The echo pattern here is compressive pericardial effusion, not acute MR. (Source: eTG complete: Post-MI mechanical complications)

Sub-acute LV free wall rupture typically presents 3 to 7 days post-MI with tamponade physiology (JVP up, y-descent absent, hypotension, RV diastolic collapse on echo) and a falling haemoglobin without external bleeding. Definitive treatment is emergency surgical repair; pericardiocentesis can transiently relieve tamponade but reduces the compressive haemostasis and risks accelerated rebleeding. Antiplatelet load and dual antiplatelet therapy amplify the risk. (Source: eTG complete: Post-MI mechanical complications)

explanation.summary: This is warfarin-related intracerebral haemorrhage requiring immediate reversal. The NBA Australian pathway for life-threatening bleeding on warfarin is prothrombinex-VF 50 IU/kg IV plus vitamin K 5-10 mg IV, with repeat INR at 30 minutes; FFP is added if prothrombinex is unavailable or if INR remains elevated. Vitamin K alone is too slow, FFP alone has slower onset and volume risk, recombinant factor VIIa is not indicated for warfarin, and idarucizumab is specific to dabigatran.
key_points: NBA warfarin reversal (life-threatening bleed): prothrombinex-VF 50 IU/kg IV plus vitamin K 5-10 mg IV
Repeat INR at 30 minutes and re-dose if needed
FFP is second-line or add-on, not first-line in Australia
Idarucizumab is dabigatran reversal, not warfarin
explanation.pearls: For any warfarin-related intracranial haemorrhage, prothrombinex 50 IU/kg plus vitamin K 5-10 mg IV within 30 minutes is your target; do not spend the first hour on FFP alone.

options.rationale: Vitamin K alone takes 6-12 hours to lower INR meaningfully and does not immediately restore clotting factors; in life-threatening bleeding, prothrombinex is needed to achieve factor replacement within minutes. Vitamin K must still be given but as an adjunct, not sole therapy. (Source: NBA Warfarin reversal guideline)

NBA Australian warfarin reversal for life-threatening bleeding (including intracerebral haemorrhage) is prothrombinex-VF 50 IU/kg IV (weight-banded in some protocols) plus vitamin K 5-10 mg IV, with repeat INR at 30 minutes; add fresh frozen plasma 150-300 mL if prothrombinex is unavailable or if the INR remains elevated. (Source: NBA Warfarin reversal guideline)

FFP alone requires 4-6 units for adequate factor replacement, has slower onset than prothrombinex, and carries greater volume load; prothrombinex is preferred first-line in AU practice. Oral vitamin K is not appropriate in life-threatening bleeding. (Source: NBA Warfarin reversal guideline)

Recombinant factor VIIa is not in the NBA warfarin reversal pathway; it carries substantial thrombotic risk and is not indicated for warfarin reversal. Prothrombinex plus vitamin K is the AU first-line for life-threatening warfarin-related bleeding. (Source: NBA Warfarin reversal guideline)

Idarucizumab is a specific dabigatran reversal agent, not warfarin. Using it for warfarin gives no reversal effect and delays appropriate prothrombinex plus vitamin K administration. (Source: NBA Warfarin reversal guideline)

explanation.summary: This is septic shock from urosepsis in a patient with a recent ureteric stent, complicated by acute kidney injury and lactic acidosis. The Surviving Sepsis hour-1 bundle mandates broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour of shock recognition, blood cultures before antibiotics (already taken), lactate measurement, and 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 4. Vasopressors are added when MAP stays under 65 after fluid resuscitation. Piperacillin-tazobactam plus gentamicin covers resistant post-stent urosepsis flora. Imaging and source control follow antibiotics and resuscitation.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: antibiotics within 1 hour of shock recognition
30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate >4 mmol/L
Vasopressors added when MAP <65 after fluid resuscitation
Piperacillin-tazobactam plus gentamicin for post-stent urosepsis (eTG)
explanation.pearls: In septic shock, antibiotics and fluids run in parallel within the first hour; save vasopressors for after fluid, and never delay antibiotics for imaging or source control planning.

options.rationale: Vasopressors are added when MAP remains under 65 despite adequate fluid resuscitation, not started before antibiotics. Antibiotic priority in the first hour is paramount for shock outcomes. (Source: Surviving Sepsis 2021 / eTG Antibiotic)

Delaying antibiotics for 3 hours is inconsistent with the hour-1 bundle, which mandates antibiotics within 1 hour of shock recognition. Fluid and antibiotics run in parallel, not sequentially. Ceftriaxone monotherapy also under-covers resistant post-stent flora. (Source: Surviving Sepsis 2021 / eTG Antibiotic)

Surviving Sepsis hour-1 bundle: give broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour of septic shock recognition, and start a 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus for hypotension or lactate above 4. Piperacillin-tazobactam plus gentamicin covers Gram-negative and Gram-positive urosepsis and the resistant flora often present after a recent stent. Vasopressors are added if MAP under 65 after fluid. (Source: Surviving Sepsis 2021 / eTG Antibiotic)

Imaging is important to identify source control needs but must not delay antibiotics or resuscitation in septic shock; antibiotics and fluids run first, imaging follows. (Source: Surviving Sepsis 2021 / eTG Antibiotic)

500 mL bolus is well under the 30 mL/kg recommended for septic shock; underfluid resuscitation prolongs shock. Meropenem monotherapy is broader than typically needed for urosepsis in Australia (eTG piperacillin-tazobactam plus gentamicin is the standard). (Source: Surviving Sepsis 2021 / eTG Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: This is postmenopausal osteoporosis with a minimal-trauma distal radius fracture and T scores under -2.5 at the femoral neck and lumbar spine. Australian first-line pharmacotherapy is an oral bisphosphonate (alendronate 70 mg weekly), taken upright with water 30 minutes before food. Vitamin D and calcium are adequate at baseline. Denosumab is second-line due to rebound vertebral fracture risk on discontinuation; teriparatide is reserved for very high risk patients; strontium ranelate has been restricted for cardiovascular reasons; and raloxifene is a later-line SERM.
key_points: First-line for postmenopausal osteoporosis with minimal-trauma fracture: oral bisphosphonate
Take alendronate 70 mg weekly upright 30 min before food with water
Denosumab has rebound vertebral fracture risk on discontinuation
Teriparatide reserved for very high risk (T -3.0 with 2+ fractures on bisphosphonate)
explanation.pearls: For a first fragility fracture with a T score of -2.5 or worse, oral alendronate 70 mg weekly is the AU default; save denosumab for oral intolerance or contraindication.

options.rationale: Strontium ranelate has been withdrawn or restricted in many jurisdictions because of cardiovascular risk and has fallen out of first-line use. It is not the AU first-line for osteoporosis. (Source: Osteoporosis Australia/RACGP MSK guidelines)

Denosumab is very effective but is not routine first-line in Australia because of the rebound vertebral fracture risk on discontinuation; PBS restriction is for patients who cannot tolerate or have contraindications to oral bisphosphonates. It is preferred second-line. (Source: Osteoporosis Australia/RACGP MSK guidelines)

Teriparatide is a PBS-restricted anabolic reserved for very high fracture risk (T score under -3.0 with 2 or more fractures on bisphosphonate) or for severe glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis; first-line therapy is oral alendronate for this patient. (Source: Osteoporosis Australia/RACGP MSK guidelines)

For postmenopausal osteoporosis with a minimal-trauma fracture and T score under -2.5, alendronate 70 mg weekly is first-line per Australian osteoporosis guidance because it is inexpensive, PBS-listed, and has robust anti-fracture data. Take upright with water 30 minutes before food. Vitamin D and calcium sufficient at baseline. (Source: Osteoporosis Australia/RACGP MSK guidelines)

Raloxifene is a second or third-line option and increases venous thromboembolism risk; it is not first-line for postmenopausal osteoporosis with a fragility fracture. Bisphosphonate is preferred first-line. (Source: Osteoporosis Australia/RACGP MSK guidelines)

explanation.summary: This is Stanford type A aortic dissection (flap starts in the ascending aorta) with aortic regurgitation and BP asymmetry. Type A is a surgical emergency with mortality of 1 percent per hour untreated. Medical bridging aims to reduce shear stress: beta-blocker FIRST (esmolol infusion to HR under 60) to lower dP/dt, then a vasodilator (nitroprusside or GTN) to bring systolic BP to 100-120 mmHg while cardiothoracic surgery is arranged. Vasodilator alone causes reflex tachycardia and worsens propagation. Antiplatelet loading, thrombolysis, and diuretic-first strategies are all incorrect and harmful.
key_points: Type A dissection = surgical emergency; type B usually medical
Medical bridging: beta-blocker first (HR <60), then vasodilator (SBP 100-120)
Antiplatelet loading and thrombolysis are contraindicated
Vasodilator without beta-blockade causes reflex tachycardia and propagation
explanation.pearls: In aortic dissection, always beta-block BEFORE giving nitroprusside; giving nitroprusside first causes reflex tachycardia that extends the flap.

options.rationale: This is a Stanford type A dissection (starts in ascending aorta) and is a surgical emergency; medical management aims to reduce shear stress with beta-blockade FIRST to lower dP/dt, then a vasodilator to bring systolic BP to about 100-120 mmHg while awaiting operative repair. Nitroprusside without prior beta-blockade risks reflex tachycardia worsening shear stress. Aortic root repair is definitive. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular: Aortic dissection)

The flap starts in the ascending aorta making this Stanford type A, not type B. Type A dissection is a surgical emergency (30 percent mortality per day untreated) not amenable to medical management alone. Labetalol is appropriate but the disposition is theatre, not conservative admission. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular: Aortic dissection)

Thrombolysis in aortic dissection is catastrophic (accelerates the dissection and causes tamponade or exsanguination). The tearing pain radiating to the back plus widened mediastinum plus BP asymmetry point to dissection not STEMI, and the ECG is not diagnostic of STEMI. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular: Aortic dissection)

Aspirin plus clopidogrel dual antiplatelet therapy in aortic dissection worsens haemorrhage and delays operative repair. Anticoagulation and antiplatelet loading are contraindicated. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular: Aortic dissection)

Nitrate without beta-blockade causes reflex tachycardia and worsens dissection propagation; the priority is beta-blockade first (esmolol or labetalol) then a vasodilator. Furosemide is not indicated in dissection unless overt pulmonary oedema is present. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular: Aortic dissection)

explanation.summary: This is necrotising fasciitis with sepsis (pain out of proportion, dusky discoloration beyond erythema, haemorrhagic bulla, sensory loss, LRINEC 8). Management is IMMEDIATE surgical debridement plus broad empirical antibiotics including clindamycin for streptococcal toxin suppression. The eTG empirical regimen is piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin (for MRSA) plus clindamycin. Every hour of delay to surgery raises mortality; imaging should not delay theatre when clinical features are strong. HBO is an adjunct at best, not a substitute for surgery.
key_points: Nec fasc clinical clues: pain out of proportion, dusky discoloration beyond erythema, bullae, sensory loss
LRINEC score >=8 is high probability
Empirical antibiotics: piperacillin-tazobactam + vancomycin + clindamycin (toxin suppression)
Immediate surgical debridement is the cornerstone; imaging must not delay theatre
explanation.pearls: In suspected nec fasc, activate theatre before finalising imaging; the LRINEC and clinical picture are enough, and every hour of delay adds mortality.

sources.label: ANZAS surgical guidelines: Necrotising soft tissue infection

options.rationale: Imaging is helpful when the diagnosis is uncertain but should NEVER delay surgical review or theatre when clinical features and LRINEC are strongly suggestive; absence of gas on imaging does NOT exclude nec fasc. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Necrotising fasciitis)

Flucloxacillin monotherapy under-covers polymicrobial necrotising fasciitis and does not suppress streptococcal toxin production. Watching and waiting is fatal in nec fasc; the LRINEC of 8 and clinical picture mandate immediate surgery. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Necrotising fasciitis)

Ceftriaxone monotherapy is insufficient for nec fasc and treating this as cellulitis with elective review delays theatre. Overnight delay in a septic nec fasc patient is fatal. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Necrotising fasciitis)

This is necrotising fasciitis (pain out of proportion, hazy dusky discoloration beyond erythema, haemorrhagic bulla, sensory loss, LRINEC 8) with sepsis. Definitive management is EARLY surgical debridement in theatre alongside broad empirical antibiotics including clindamycin for toxin suppression. Piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin plus clindamycin is the standard eTG Australian empirical regimen. Every hour of delay to surgery raises mortality. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Necrotising fasciitis)

Hyperbaric oxygen may be an adjunct AFTER surgical debridement and antibiotics; it does NOT replace or precede surgery. Delaying debridement to arrange HBO is contraindicated. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Necrotising fasciitis)

explanation.summary: This is anaphylaxis refractory to two IM adrenaline doses in a patient on chronic beta-blocker therapy. ASCIA escalates to IV adrenaline infusion titrated to response after two IM doses fail. When beta-blocker mediated adrenaline resistance is suspected, IV glucagon 1-2 mg is the standard adjunct because it increases cAMP independent of beta-adrenergic receptors. Steroids, antihistamines, nebulised adrenaline, and noradrenaline all have supporting or adjunct roles but do not replace escalation of adrenaline and glucagon in this scenario.
key_points: After 2 IM adrenaline doses without response: IV adrenaline infusion
Beta-blocker on board: give IV glucagon 1-2 mg for adrenaline resistance
Steroids and antihistamines are adjuncts, not primary treatment
Noradrenaline is a later add-on for refractory shock unresponsive to adrenaline
explanation.pearls: In an anaphylactic patient on beta-blockers not responding to IM adrenaline, IV glucagon 1-2 mg alongside IV adrenaline infusion is the way to unlock the beta-adrenergic blockade.

options.rationale: After two IM doses without response, ASCIA advises escalating to IV adrenaline infusion rather than a third IM. Continuing crystalloid without escalation of adrenaline delays effective treatment. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

After two IM adrenaline doses without adequate response, ASCIA recommends IV adrenaline infusion. In a patient on beta-blockers who is failing to respond, IV glucagon 1-2 mg (which acts on cAMP independent of beta-adrenergic receptors) is the standard adjunct to overcome beta-blocker resistance. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

Steroids and antihistamines are adjuncts and do not treat the acute cardiovascular collapse; they should not delay escalation to IV adrenaline in refractory anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

Noradrenaline can be used as adjunct for refractory anaphylactic shock unresponsive to adrenaline, but IV adrenaline infusion is the first escalation after IM failure. Skipping adrenaline for noradrenaline is not standard. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

Nebulised adrenaline treats upper airway oedema but does not treat systemic anaphylactic shock; salbutamol and hydrocortisone are adjuncts. None of these address the beta-blocker-mediated adrenaline resistance that is the barrier here. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

explanation.summary: This patient is high-risk for TLS (Burkitt lymphoma with bulky disease, LDH more than 4 times upper limit, and baseline uric acid above upper limit). eviQ and HSANZ recommend rasburicase (0.2 mg/kg IV as a single dose or a fixed-dose regimen) for high-risk TLS because it converts uric acid to allantoin within hours, unlike allopurinol which only blocks new formation and takes 48-72 hours. G6PD deficiency is a contraindication to rasburicase due to haemolysis risk; screening was normal here. Hyperhydration continues but urinary alkalinisation with bicarbonate is no longer recommended because it worsens calcium phosphate precipitation. Prophylactic dialysis is not routine.
key_points: High-risk TLS (Burkitt, bulky disease, LDH >4x ULN, high urate): rasburicase
Screen G6PD before rasburicase (contraindicated in deficiency)
Urinary alkalinisation with bicarbonate is NOT recommended
Allopurinol only blocks new urate formation; slow onset (48-72 hours)
explanation.pearls: For high-risk TLS in Burkitt lymphoma with a G6PD-normal patient, rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg IV drops existing urate within hours; do not waste time on allopurinol prophylaxis alone.

options.rationale: Allopurinol prevents new uric acid formation but does NOT treat the existing high uric acid; it takes 48-72 hours to lower urate meaningfully. For high-risk TLS (Burkitt with bulky disease, LDH >4 times upper limit, and baseline urate above upper limit) rasburicase is preferred as it degrades existing uric acid within hours. (Source: eviQ tumour lysis syndrome / HSANZ)

Prophylactic dialysis is only indicated when established renal failure or refractory hyperkalaemia or hyperphosphataemia occurs during TLS; it is not routine prophylaxis. Rasburicase plus aggressive hydration prevents most cases from progressing to dialysis. (Source: eviQ tumour lysis syndrome / HSANZ)

Febuxostat is an alternative to allopurinol but is not preferred over rasburicase for high-risk TLS. Urinary alkalinisation with bicarbonate is NO LONGER recommended because it worsens calcium phosphate precipitation and increases xanthine crystallisation. (Source: eviQ tumour lysis syndrome / HSANZ)

Burkitt lymphoma with bulky disease, LDH more than 4 times upper limit, and elevated baseline uric acid places this patient in the high-risk TLS category. eviQ and HSANZ pathways recommend rasburicase as first-line uric acid lowering because it converts uric acid to allantoin within hours, unlike allopurinol which only blocks new formation. G6PD deficiency (haemolysis risk) has been excluded. Hyperhydration with balanced crystalloid continues. (Source: eviQ tumour lysis syndrome / HSANZ)

Burkitt lymphoma has extremely rapid doubling time; delaying chemotherapy for prophylaxis without addressing the immediate uric acid risk is dangerous. Rasburicase allows chemotherapy to start on schedule while managing hyperuricaemia. Alkalinisation is not recommended. (Source: eviQ tumour lysis syndrome / HSANZ)

explanation.summary: In STEMI, primary PCI is preferred when it can be delivered within 120 minutes of first medical contact. Beyond this window, weight-adjusted bolus tenecteplase (with enoxaparin and clopidogrel or ticagrelor as per local protocol) is given without delay, followed by early transfer to a PCI centre for rescue PCI if reperfusion fails or routine coronary angiography at 3 to 24 hours (pharmacoinvasive strategy). Waiting for troponin or omitting reperfusion is inappropriate.
key_points: Primary PCI preferred if within 120 min of first medical contact
Otherwise fibrinolysis with tenecteplase then transfer
Rescue PCI if failed reperfusion; routine angiography 3 to 24 hours
STEMI diagnosis is ECG-based; do not wait for troponin
explanation.pearls: Failed reperfusion after fibrinolysis is defined as under 50 percent ST resolution at 60 to 90 minutes, ongoing chest pain, or haemodynamic instability; these mandate immediate rescue PCI, not repeat lytics.

options.rationale: Transfer for primary PCI is only preferred when total delay to PCI is under 120 minutes from first medical contact; 3 hours by road plus door-to-balloon exceeds this window, so lytics are preferred.

STEMI diagnosis is ECG-based; waiting for troponin delays reperfusion. Not offering reperfusion at all is inappropriate for STEMI within 12 hours of symptom onset in a patient without contraindications.

Streptokinase is rarely used in Australia due to inferior patency rates and allergy risk; tenecteplase is the preferred fibrinolytic. Transfer should also occur to allow rescue PCI if reperfusion fails.
