When primary PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes of first medical contact, prehospital or in-hospital fibrinolysis with weight-adjusted tenecteplase is preferred, followed by early transfer for pharmacoinvasive PCI.
Nitrates and beta-blockers do not reperfuse the coronary artery; reperfusion is the priority in STEMI within 12 hours of symptom onset in a patient without contraindications to thrombolysis.

explanation.summary: Moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring hospital admission is treated in Australia with IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily to cover atypicals. Once the patient is clinically stable (afebrile 24 hours, tolerating oral, improving inflammatory markers, no hypoxia), switch to oral amoxicillin 1 g TDS plus doxycycline for a total 7 day course. Broad-spectrum agents are reserved for severe disease or specific risk factors.
key_points: Moderate CAP: IV benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline
Switch to oral when clinically stable; total 7 days
CURB-65 useful for severity but adverse features (hypoxia, RR) also decide admission
Broad-spectrum only for severe disease or specific risk factors
explanation.pearls: IV to oral switch is safe when the patient has stable vitals for 24 hours, is tolerating oral, is haemodynamically stable, has improving CRP and WCC, and there is no pleural infection; do not wait for the CXR to clear.

options.rationale: Home management may be acceptable for very low severity (CURB-65 0 to 1 with no adverse features) but hypoxia at SpO2 91 percent and RR 26 are adverse features so hospital IV therapy is preferred.
Broad spectrum cover with anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam is reserved for severe pneumonia or specific risk factors (structural lung disease, healthcare exposure) and is not first line for moderate CAP.
Vancomycin is added only when there is necrotising pneumonia, cavitation or specific MRSA risk factors; empirical addition for community-acquired pneumonia is inappropriate as first-line therapy.
Moxifloxacin monotherapy for CAP has QT and mycobacterial concerns; oseltamivir requires evidence of influenza; home management with hypoxia at SpO2 91 percent is not safe management.

AU eTG for moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring hospitalisation is IV benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline, switching to oral therapy once clinically stable, tolerating oral, and improving inflammatory markers.

explanation.summary: For atrial fibrillation on warfarin without mechanical valve, recent stroke, recent VTE, or CHA2DS2-VASc of 7 or more, the BRIDGE trial showed no benefit to LMWH bridging and increased bleeding risk. Stop warfarin 5 days before surgery, do not bridge, and restart warfarin 12 to 24 hours after surgery when haemostasis is achieved. Vitamin K acceleration causes postoperative warfarin resistance and should be avoided routinely.
key_points: No bridging for AF unless mechanical valve, recent stroke, recent VTE or CHA2DS2-VASc 7+
Stop warfarin 5 days pre-op
Restart warfarin 12 to 24 hours post-op when haemostasis achieved
Routine oral vitamin K causes postoperative warfarin resistance
explanation.pearls: Full-dose bridging LMWH is contraindicated within 24 hours of major surgery and is generally started 3 days before and stopped 24 hours before; prophylactic-dose LMWH can be used postoperatively for surgical VTE prophylaxis.

options.rationale: For atrial fibrillation without mechanical valve, prior stroke or recent VTE, BRIDGE trial evidence shows no bridging is preferred; bridging LMWH increases bleeding without reducing stroke.
Elective knee arthroplasty is a high bleeding risk procedure; warfarin must be held perioperatively to avoid intra- and postoperative bleeding requiring transfusion and reoperation.
Full-dose bridging is reserved for very high thromboembolic risk (mechanical mitral valve, recent stroke or VTE under 3 months, CHA2DS2-VASc 7 or more); this patient does not meet those criteria.
Routine oral vitamin K creates warfarin resistance postoperatively, delaying re-anticoagulation; 5 days off warfarin without vitamin K reliably normalises the INR in most patients.
Switching between anticoagulants perioperatively adds complexity and cost without benefit, introducing a gap or overlap; simple hold of warfarin is the standard perioperative strategy.

explanation.summary: SIADH diagnostic criteria are met with euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia (plasma osm below 275), inappropriately concentrated urine (urine osm above 100), and urine sodium above 30 mmol/L, with normal thyroid and adrenal function, no diuretic use and no volume depletion. First-line management is fluid restriction 800 to 1000 mL/day; hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic disease. Correction is limited to under 8 mmol/L per 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination.
key_points: SIADH: euvolaemic, plasma osm low, urine osm > 100, urine Na > 30, normal TFTs and cortisol
First line: fluid restrict 800 to 1000 mL/day
Isotonic saline can paradoxically worsen SIADH
Correct no more than 8 mmol/L in 24 hours; hypertonic saline only for severe symptoms
explanation.pearls: If overcorrection occurs (sodium rises more than 8 mmol/L in 24 hours), stop all sodium sources, administer 5 percent dextrose IV, and consider desmopressin 2 microgram IV to prevent osmotic demyelination.

sources.label: European Society of Endocrinology hyponatraemia guideline

options.rationale: Isotonic saline in SIADH can paradoxically worsen hyponatraemia because urine osmolality (480) exceeds infused osmolality; water is retained while sodium is excreted in the urine.
source_refs: European Society of Endocrinology hyponatraemia guideline

options.rationale: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine and euvolaemia meets SIADH criteria; first-line management is fluid restriction (800 to 1000 mL/day) with monitoring and limiting correction to under 8 mmol/L per 24 hours.
source_refs: European Society of Endocrinology hyponatraemia guideline

options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, coma, severe drowsiness); this patient has only mild symptoms and can be managed with fluid restriction first.
source_refs: European Society of Endocrinology hyponatraemia guideline

options.rationale: Demeclocycline is now rarely used due to nephrotoxicity and slow onset; tolvaptan is preferred if pharmacotherapy is needed after fluid restriction has failed to produce an adequate response.
source_refs: European Society of Endocrinology hyponatraemia guideline

options.rationale: Furosemide plus salt tablets is a niche second-line strategy in SIADH; not first line and carries a risk of overcorrection and electrolyte disturbance without benefit over fluid restriction.
source_refs: European Society of Endocrinology hyponatraemia guideline

explanation.summary: HHS differs from DKA in that acidosis and significant ketosis are absent, and effective osmolality is markedly raised (over 320 mOsm/kg). Management prioritises IV fluid resuscitation with 0.9 percent saline (1 L in the first hour then reassess), which alone usually reduces glucose by 5 mmol/L per hour. Insulin is started at low dose (0.05 units/kg/hour) and delayed until glucose ceases falling with fluids. Target correction is 5 mmol/L per hour fall.
key_points: HHS: acidosis absent, ketones minimal, effective osmolality > 320
Fluid resuscitation is primary; insulin low-dose and delayed
Target glucose fall 5 mmol/L per hour, not 10
Rapid osmolar correction causes cerebral oedema and haemodynamic collapse
explanation.pearls: HHS has a mortality of 15 to 20 percent compared with 1 to 5 percent for DKA; identifying and treating the precipitant (commonly infection, myocardial infarction, medication non-adherence) is crucial.

sources.label: JBDS-IP: Management of hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state

options.rationale: HHS: give fluid first (1 L over 1 hour, reassess), start insulin low-dose 0.05 units/kg/hour and only after several hours when glucose ceases falling with fluids; rapid insulin causes cerebral oedema.
source_refs: JBDS-IP: Management of hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state

options.rationale: 0.1 units/kg/hour is the DKA regimen; in HHS this rate causes too-rapid osmotic shifts leading to cerebral oedema and cardiovascular collapse. Target glucose fall in HHS is 5 mmol/L per hour.
source_refs: JBDS-IP: Management of hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state

options.rationale: AU HHS management: aggressive but careful isotonic fluid is primary; insulin is low-dose (0.05 units/kg/hour) and delayed, only added when glucose stops falling with fluids alone, targeting 5 mmol/L fall per hour.
source_refs: JBDS-IP: Management of hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state

options.rationale: 5 percent dextrose worsens hyperglycaemia; insulin bolus is not recommended in DKA or HHS; targeting 8 mmol/L within 4 hours is far too rapid an osmolar correction for HHS management.
source_refs: JBDS-IP: Management of hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state

options.rationale: Subcutaneous long-acting insulin has slow onset and cannot be titrated in an acutely unwell patient; IV insulin infusion (once fluid-resuscitated and if needed) is required for HHS.
source_refs: JBDS-IP: Management of hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state

explanation.summary: Contrast-induced nephropathy prevention in high-risk patients (eGFR under 45, diabetes, heart failure, ACEi/ARB/diuretics/NSAIDs) requires withholding nephrotoxic medications and temporary cessation of metformin because of lactic acidosis risk. IV isotonic saline at 1 mL/kg/hour is given for 12 hours before and 12 hours after the procedure. The lowest effective iso-osmolar or low-osmolar contrast volume should be used. N-acetylcysteine and sodium bicarbonate are not superior to saline hydration (PRESERVE trial 2018) and are no longer recommended.
key_points: Withhold metformin (day of contrast); recheck creatinine at 48 hours before resuming
Withhold ACEi/ARB/diuretics peri-procedure in high-risk patients
IV isotonic saline 1 mL/kg/hour 12 hours pre and post
Use lowest effective iso-osmolar contrast volume
explanation.pearls: Post-contrast acute kidney injury is now considered rarer than previously for IV studies, but the highest-risk group remains diabetics with eGFR under 30 or acute kidney injury; radiologist and cardiologist should be informed to minimise volume.

options.rationale: Recent evidence (PRESERVE trial) shows no benefit of N-acetylcysteine over placebo for contrast-induced nephropathy prevention; it is no longer recommended in contemporary practice guidelines.

Metformin should be temporarily held from the day of contrast when eGFR is under 60 until renal function is confirmed stable 48 hours later, due to lactic acidosis risk; ACEi and diuretics are also usually held.

Sodium bicarbonate is non-superior to isotonic saline for CIN prevention (PRESERVE); IV isotonic saline hydration is the standard first-line prophylaxis in patients with additional risk factors like diabetes.

AU KHA-CARI approach for eGFR 30 to 45 with additional risk factors (diabetes, HF, ACEi, diuretics): withhold nephrotoxic and metformin drugs, provide 12-hour peri-procedural isotonic saline hydration, minimise contrast volume with iso-osmolar agent.
Invasive coronary angiography uses more contrast than CT; MRI does not replace anatomical coronary imaging. Preventive strategies allow the CT to proceed safely in most patients at risk.

explanation.summary: In septic shock with a history of ESBL infection in the past 6 months, empirical antibiotic cover should include a carbapenem (meropenem 1 g every 8 hours, dose-adjusted for creatinine clearance). Piperacillin-tazobactam is inferior to meropenem for ESBL bacteraemia (MERINO trial 2018). Blood and urine cultures should be obtained before antibiotics only if this does not delay administration beyond 45 minutes. Septic shock unresponsive to 2 L of fluid warrants ICU-level care and vasopressor consideration.
key_points: ESBL history in the past 6 months: cover empirically with a carbapenem
Piperacillin-tazobactam inferior to meropenem for ESBL bacteraemia (MERINO)
Cultures before antibiotics only if no delay beyond 45 minutes
Septic shock unresponsive to 2 L fluid: escalate to ICU and vasopressors
explanation.pearls: For a patient with ESBL history but who is haemodynamically stable and not septic, oral fosfomycin 3 g single dose or oral pivmecillinam are options for uncomplicated ESBL cystitis, sparing carbapenems.

sources.label: MERINO trial: piperacillin-tazobactam vs meropenem for ESBL

options.rationale: Amoxicillin plus gentamicin does not reliably cover ESBL organisms; empirical cover for a patient with recent ESBL infection and septic shock must include a carbapenem for adequate empirical activity.
Ceftriaxone will not cover ESBL organisms which produce enzymes that hydrolyse third-generation cephalosporins; ward-based care is inappropriate for septic shock unresponsive to initial 2 L fluids.
Piperacillin-tazobactam has poor reliability in ESBL bacteraemia (MERINO trial showed higher mortality vs meropenem); ICU-level care is required for shock unresponsive to fluid resuscitation.
Vancomycin plus metronidazole covers gram-positive and anaerobic infection but does not cover ESBL gram-negative pathogens driving her urosepsis, and misses the causative organism entirely today.

For septic shock with recent history of ESBL urosepsis, empirical carbapenem cover (meropenem) is appropriate and dose-adjusted; cultures should be taken before antibiotics if this does not delay administration beyond 45 minutes.

explanation.summary: Latent tuberculosis infection in a person from a high-incidence country with a positive interferon-gamma release assay, clear chest X-ray and no symptoms warrants offered treatment to prevent reactivation. AU preferred regimens are 3HR (rifampicin plus isoniazid for 3 months) or 4R (rifampicin monotherapy for 4 months), with pyridoxine to prevent isoniazid neuropathy. Monthly LFT monitoring and hepatitis symptom review during treatment are standard. 9H is a legacy regimen with lower completion rates.
key_points: Positive QFT-Plus with clear XR and no symptoms = LTBI
3HR is AU preferred regimen (or 4R if isoniazid contraindicated)
Pyridoxine prevents INH peripheral neuropathy
Monthly LFTs and hepatitis symptom check during treatment
explanation.pearls: Rifampicin induces CYP3A4 and reduces efficacy of combined hormonal contraception, warfarin and many antiretrovirals; alternative contraception (copper IUD, DMPA) is planned before starting a rifampicin-containing regimen in women of reproductive age.

options.rationale: AU CDNA and TSANZ latent TB treatment recommends 3HR (3 month rifampicin plus isoniazid) as preferred regimen due to shorter duration, better completion and equal efficacy to 6H; pyridoxine prevents peripheral neuropathy.
9H is a legacy regimen; AU has moved to shorter regimens (3HR or 4R) as first-line to improve completion rates.
4R is an accepted alternative if isoniazid contraindicated; when both agents can be given, 3HR is preferred as shorter than 4R in AU pathways.
Recent migration from a high-incidence country and known household contact confer a lifetime reactivation risk of 5 to 10 percent; treatment materially reduces this and is offered per AU guidance.
In a person with known past exposure, single QFT-Plus positive is sufficient for LTBI diagnosis; repeat delays treatment without changing management.

explanation.summary: Suspected Cushing syndrome is screened with one of three first-line tests: overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test, 24-hour urinary free cortisol (two collections), or late-night salivary cortisol (two samples). A positive screen requires a second abnormal test from the panel to confirm hypercortisolism before proceeding to ACTH and localisation. Single morning cortisol and pituitary MRI are not initial screens because they lack specificity or lead to incidentalomas.
key_points: 1 mg overnight DST is a first-line Cushing screen
Alternatives: 24 hr UFC (x2), late-night salivary cortisol (x2)
Need two abnormal tests before diagnostic confirmation
ACTH and imaging follow biochemical confirmation, not precede it
explanation.pearls: Common causes of false-positive DST include pregnancy, oestrogen therapy (raises CBG), rifampicin (accelerates dexamethasone metabolism), depression, chronic alcohol use and severe illness; check for these before pursuing confirmatory workup on an isolated abnormal screen.

options.rationale: ACTH is used to distinguish ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent Cushing after screening confirms hypercortisolism; not the first screen.
1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test is a first-line Endocrine Society AU-endorsed screen for Cushing syndrome; morning cortisol above 50 nmol/L is abnormal and prompts confirmatory testing.
Single morning cortisol has poor discrimination for Cushing; loss of diurnal rhythm and failure to suppress on DST are the screening tests.
ARR screens for primary aldosteronism, not Cushing; her clinical features (central obesity, striae, proximal weakness, plethora) point to Cushing.
Imaging follows biochemical confirmation; up to 10 percent of the population has incidental pituitary microadenomas so pre-biochemistry MRI misleads.

explanation.summary: Post-menopausal osteoporosis with a fragility fracture, T-score <=-2.5 at hip or spine, or chronic glucocorticoid exposure warrants first-line oral bisphosphonate therapy (alendronate 70 mg weekly or risedronate 35 mg weekly) with calcium and vitamin D optimisation, dental review to reduce MRONJ risk, and 5-yearly reassessment. IV zoledronate is second-line for intolerance. Denosumab is an alternative but requires follow-on antiresorptive on cessation. Teriparatide is reserved for severe or bisphosphonate-refractory disease.
key_points: First-line pharmacotherapy: oral alendronate or risedronate
Dental review before bisphosphonate for MRONJ risk mitigation
IV zoledronate second-line if oral intolerance
Denosumab needs follow-on bisphosphonate to prevent rebound fractures
explanation.pearls: Bisphosphonate holiday after 5 years of oral therapy is considered for low-risk patients but not for those with continuing high risk (prior vertebral fracture, femoral neck T -2.5, ongoing glucocorticoid use); a repeat DEXA and clinical assessment guide the decision.

options.rationale: IV zoledronate is used when oral bisphosphonates are not tolerated or absorbed; oral alendronate is first-line in AU. Dental review remains prudent before any bisphosphonate.

Denosumab is a valid option but not first-line before an oral bisphosphonate trial; and it must be followed by a bisphosphonate on cessation to prevent rebound vertebral fractures, requiring long-term planning.
Teriparatide is used after antiresorptive failure or in severe osteoporosis with vertebral fractures; not first-line, is limited on PBS to specific criteria, and has an 18 to 24 month lifetime cap.

Post-menopausal osteoporosis with prior fragility fracture is a clear indication for oral bisphosphonate; alendronate is first-line PBS-listed with dental review before initiation for MRONJ risk mitigation.
Calcium and vitamin D alone do not reduce fracture risk sufficiently in established osteoporosis after fragility fracture; pharmacotherapy is required.

explanation.summary: Modified Duke criteria diagnose definite infective endocarditis when there are 2 major (typical organism in 2+ blood cultures, echocardiographic evidence of endocardial involvement), or 1 major plus 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria. AU regimen for streptococcal prosthetic valve endocarditis is benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV every 4 hours plus low-dose gentamicin 3 mg/kg daily for 6 weeks. Prosthetic valve endocarditis mandates transoesophageal echocardiogram, cardiothoracic surgical review and colonoscopy for S. gallolyticus.
key_points: Modified Duke: 2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor = definite
Streptococcal PVE: benzylpenicillin + gentamicin 6 weeks
S. gallolyticus mandates colonoscopy for occult colorectal cancer
PVE always needs TOE and cardiothoracic surgical review
explanation.pearls: Surgical indications for infective endocarditis include heart failure from valve dysfunction, uncontrolled infection despite adequate antibiotics after 5 to 7 days, large vegetations (>10 mm) with embolic phenomena and paravalvular abscess or dehiscence; early surgery in the first week improves outcomes when these are present.

options.rationale: Vancomycin monotherapy is not optimal for penicillin-susceptible streptococcal endocarditis and delaying TOE plus surgical consult in prosthetic valve endocarditis with regurgitation risks disease progression.

Prosthetic valve endocarditis warrants combination therapy with gentamicin for 2 to 6 weeks under AU guidelines; and cardiothoracic surgical consultation is mandatory in prosthetic valve endocarditis for shared surgical decision making.

This meets modified Duke definite endocarditis (two major: positive typical organism and vegetation on echo); AU regimen for streptococcal PVE is benzylpenicillin plus low-dose gentamicin; S. gallolyticus mandates colonoscopy for occult colorectal cancer.
Culture is confirmed as S. gallolyticus, not S. aureus; flucloxacillin does not cover streptococci and rifampicin is only added for staphylococcal PVE, not streptococcal.

PVE in the first 12 months post surgery does not have the microbiology of community endocarditis and needs inpatient management for at least the first 2 weeks per AU guidance; and piperacillin-tazobactam is not the streptococcal PVE regimen.

explanation.summary: Primary adrenal insufficiency in crisis presents with hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and hyperpigmentation from ACTH excess. Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome (with Hashimoto thyroiditis) is a classical association. Immediate management is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 200 mg over 24 hours infusion, IV normal saline for volume, dextrose for hypoglycaemia and treat any precipitant. Levothyroxine is held until glucocorticoid replacement is established to prevent worsening the crisis.
key_points: Hyperpigmentation + hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia = primary adrenal insufficiency
IV hydrocortisone stat then 24 hr infusion is life-saving
Normal saline not Hartmann; dextrose for hypoglycaemia
Hold levothyroxine until glucocorticoid replacement established
explanation.pearls: Short synacthen test (250 microgram synthetic ACTH with cortisol at 0 and 30 min, expecting a peak above 500 nmol/L) confirms the diagnosis when done at least 24 hours after any hydrocortisone dose or by using dexamethasone as bridging therapy in the interim to avoid interference.

options.rationale: Hartmann contains potassium which may worsen hyperkalaemia in acute adrenal crisis; and dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity so hydrocortisone is preferred.
Increasing levothyroxine before glucocorticoid replacement in adrenal insufficiency precipitates further crisis by increasing cortisol clearance; hydrocortisone must be given first.
Insulin risks worsening hypoglycaemia in a hypoglycaemic patient; the definitive treatment is hydrocortisone and saline which correct all three electrolyte and glucose derangements.
Adrenal crisis is a clinical diagnosis and treatment is empirical before confirmation; delay for a morning cortisol risks death.

Hyperpigmentation with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and hypotension in a woman with autoimmune thyroid disease is primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison) in crisis; empirical hydrocortisone before biochemical confirmation is life-saving.

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency: features include pain out of proportion to examination, systemic toxicity, crepitus and haemorrhagic bullae later. LRINEC scoring supports suspicion using CRP, WCC, sodium, creatinine, haemoglobin and glucose. Management is immediate surgical exploration and wide debridement within 1 hour, empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics (meropenem plus clindamycin for antitoxin effect), IV fluid resuscitation and ICU-level supportive care. Imaging must never delay surgery.
key_points: Pain out of proportion + crepitus + systemic toxicity = suspect necrotising fasciitis
Surgical debridement within 1 hour is the priority
Empirical meropenem + clindamycin (antitoxin)
Never delay surgery for imaging
explanation.pearls: Add IV vancomycin if MRSA is prevalent in the community or hospital, and IV benzylpenicillin plus clindamycin for suspected group A streptococcal cases (LRINEC does not distinguish types); definitive antibiotics narrow once operative cultures return.

options.rationale: Pain out of proportion, crepitus, systemic toxicity and LRINEC-high biochemistry (WCC, Na, CRP, glucose, creatinine, Hb) in a diabetic point strongly to necrotising fasciitis; surgery within an hour is the intervention that improves survival.
Cellulitis regimen misses the surgical urgency of necrotising fasciitis; pain out of proportion, crepitus and systemic toxicity mandate immediate surgical exploration.
Imaging must not delay surgery in suspected necrotising fasciitis; clinical diagnosis warrants immediate theatre for debridement and empirical antibiotics simultaneously.
HBOT is adjunctive after debridement, not before; delay of surgery to arrange HBOT costs lives, and monotherapy misses the polymicrobial nature of type I necrotising fasciitis.
Ceftriaxone monotherapy does not cover the polymicrobial spectrum or provide clindamycin's antitoxin effect; and ward observation delays life-saving debridement.

explanation.summary: Type A aortic dissection presents with abrupt tearing chest and back pain, inter-arm blood pressure differential, aortic regurgitation from proximal extension, widened mediastinum on chest X-ray and pulse deficits. Immediate management is IV beta-blockade (labetalol or esmolol) titrated to HR 60 and systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg before any vasodilator to minimise dP/dt and aortic wall shear stress; urgent CT aortogram and cardiothoracic surgical activation. Antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy is held pending imaging. Definitive management of type A is emergency open surgical repair.
key_points: Tearing pain + inter-arm BP differential + widened mediastinum = suspect dissection
Beta-blockade FIRST (target HR 60), then vasodilator (target SBP 100 to 120)
Urgent CT aortogram and cardiothoracic activation
Withhold antiplatelet and anticoagulant pending diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Type A dissection (involving the ascending aorta) is a surgical emergency with mortality rising 1 percent per hour; type B (descending only, distal to left subclavian) is managed medically unless complicated by malperfusion, rupture or refractory pain and hypertension, when thoracic endovascular aortic repair is considered.

options.rationale: Vasodilator alone increases reflex tachycardia and worsens aortic wall shear stress; beta-blockade must be given first. Antiplatelet and anticoagulant are contraindicated in suspected dissection.

The tearing pain, inter-arm BP differential, aortic regurgitation murmur and widened mediastinum are classical type A aortic dissection; the AU order is negative chronotrope and beta-blockade before vasodilator to reduce shear (dP/dt), urgent CT and cardiothoracic activation.
Angiography and anticoagulation on this NSTE presentation would kill a dissection patient; a widened mediastinum and inter-arm BP differential warrant aortogram before cath.
Hydralazine increases reflex tachycardia and shear stress in dissection; and antiplatelet loading is contraindicated. Beta-blockade first, not hydralazine.

Thrombolysis in an unrecognised dissection is invariably fatal; the ST depression here reflects demand ischaemia from coronary compromise or dissection propagation, not STEMI equivalent that meets criteria.

explanation.summary: Moderate community-acquired pneumonia in Australia (SMART-COP 3 to 4) requires hospital admission and combination antibiotic therapy targeting pneumococcus and atypical organisms. IV benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline is the Therapeutic Guidelines first-line regimen. Ceftriaxone is reserved for severe CAP or beta-lactam alternatives; broader-spectrum agents for ICU-level severity or specific risk factors.
key_points: SMART-COP >=3 = moderate; >=5 = severe warranting ICU consideration
Moderate CAP: IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g q6h + doxycycline 100 mg BD
Severe CAP or ICU: IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily + azithromycin 500 mg IV daily (moxifloxacin if pen allergy)
Switch to oral after 48 hours of clinical improvement; total 5-7 days
explanation.pearls: SMART-COP awards 2 points each for systolic <90 mmHg, SpO2 <=90%, and pH <7.35 (all considered severe features), 1 point each for the other criteria. Score >=3 predicts intensive respiratory or vasopressor support.

options.rationale: SMART-COP score is at least 3 (S=0 systolic 108, M=1 multilobar, A=1 albumin 34, R=1 respiratory rate 28, T=0, C=0, O=1 SpO2 91%, P=1 pH not <7.35 so 0) placing him in moderate to high risk. Discharging home understates severity. (Source: eTG Antibiotic CAP)

Ceftriaxone monotherapy at 1 g daily is used for uncomplicated moderate CAP requiring admission in some Australian guidelines, but the correct benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline combination is the Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic recommendation for moderate CAP without severe features. Ceftriaxone is reserved for severe CAP or when benzylpenicillin is contraindicated. (Source: eTG Antibiotic CAP)

Broad-spectrum coverage is reserved for severe CAP requiring ICU support (SMART-COP >=5) or high-risk features such as recent hospitalisation, aspiration risk with structural lung disease, or bronchiectasis. This patient does not meet these criteria. (Source: eTG Antibiotic CAP)
Macrolide monotherapy is inadequate for moderate CAP in Australia because of high pneumococcal resistance. Australian guidance uses beta-lactam plus atypical cover. (Source: eTG Antibiotic CAP)

Australian Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic first-line therapy for moderate CAP requiring admission is IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg BD (or oral clarithromycin) to cover atypicals. SMART-COP score of at least 3 places him in the moderate-to-high risk group warranting admission and IV therapy with switch to oral after 48 hours if improving. (Source: eTG Antibiotic CAP)

explanation.summary: Anticoagulation duration for VTE depends on whether the event was provoked by a major transient factor (surgery, hospitalisation, trauma), a persistent factor, cancer, or unprovoked. Proximal DVT provoked by a major transient factor is treated for 3 months and stopped. Unprovoked or persistent-risk-factor VTE is considered for indefinite therapy weighing bleeding risk. Cancer-associated VTE typically receives extended DOAC or LMWH while the cancer is active.
key_points: Proximal DVT with major transient provoking factor -> 3 months anticoagulation then stop
Unprovoked proximal DVT -> at least 3 months then consider indefinite with periodic bleed-risk review
Cancer-associated VTE -> extended DOAC (edoxaban or apixaban) or LMWH while cancer active
Extended-phase apixaban dose is 2.5 mg twice daily; rivaroxaban 10 mg daily
explanation.pearls: For provoked distal (calf) DVT, 3 months of anticoagulation is often adequate but shorter courses (6 weeks) may suffice for isolated calf DVT with a clear provoking factor and reliable serial imaging follow-up.

options.rationale: This is a proximal DVT clearly provoked by a major transient risk factor (total knee replacement with post-operative immobility). Australian and international haematology guidance (Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand; ASH 2020) recommend cessation of anticoagulation at 3 months in this scenario because the annual recurrence risk after stopping is under 3%, similar to the annual major bleeding risk on ongoing therapy. Patient counselling about recognition of recurrence and future perioperative prophylaxis is essential. (Source: THANZ VTE guidelines)

Indefinite anticoagulation is reserved for unprovoked DVT, active cancer-associated VTE, or recurrent VTE. A proximal DVT provoked by a major transient risk factor does not meet indefinite therapy criteria and exposes the patient to unnecessary bleeding risk. (Source: THANZ VTE guidelines)

The extended low-dose apixaban regimen (2.5 mg BD after initial 6 months) is used for unprovoked VTE where the decision is to continue anticoagulation but reduce bleeding risk. It does not apply to a clearly provoked VTE where cessation is preferred at 3 months. (Source: THANZ VTE guidelines)

Aspirin has been studied for extended VTE prevention (ASPIRE, WARFASA) with only modest recurrence reduction and is inferior to DOAC continuation. It is not the standard approach after cessation of anticoagulation for a provoked DVT and adds bleeding risk without clear benefit here. (Source: THANZ VTE guidelines)

Extending anticoagulation to 6 months for a proximal DVT provoked by a major transient risk factor confers no reduction in long-term recurrence relative to 3 months and adds bleeding exposure. Total therapy of 3 months is the standard duration. (Source: THANZ VTE guidelines)

explanation.summary: In hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, calcium gluconate is given first to stabilise the cardiac membrane. Insulin-glucose (with or without salbutamol) then shifts potassium into cells. Definitive removal is achieved by cessation of contributing agents, potassium-binding resins or haemodialysis. In CKD stage 4 or 5 with severe or refractory hyperkalaemia, early nephrology involvement for haemodialysis is essential.
key_points: Any hyperkalaemia with ECG changes -> calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL IV first
Then insulin 10 units IV with 50 mL 50% glucose over 20 min (monitor BSL 1-2 hourly for 6 h)
Adjunct salbutamol 10-20 mg nebulised for additional potassium shift
Definitive removal: cease offending drugs, potassium binders, haemodialysis if refractory or CKD
explanation.pearls: Insulin-glucose hypoglycaemia risk peaks 1-2 hours post-dose; monitor blood glucose for at least 6 hours after administration.

options.rationale: Insulin-glucose shifts potassium intracellularly and is a subsequent step, but does not immediately stabilise the myocardium. In the presence of ECG changes, calcium is given first because cardiac stabilisation cannot wait for the 20-30 minute onset of insulin-driven shift. (Source: eTG Fluids and Electrolytes: Hyperkalaemia)

With hyperkalaemia and ECG changes (peaked T waves, PR prolongation), calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL over 2 to 5 minutes is the first-line intervention to stabilise the cardiac membrane. Onset is within 2 to 3 minutes and duration is 30 to 60 minutes. Subsequent steps shift and remove potassium. Cease perindopril, spironolactone and slow-K; consider renal replacement early in dialysis-eligible CKD stage 4. (Source: eTG Fluids and Electrolytes: Hyperkalaemia)

Salbutamol shifts potassium intracellularly and can reduce serum potassium by 0.5 to 1 mmol/L, but the onset is 15 to 30 minutes and it does not stabilise the myocardium during that window. It is adjunctive after calcium and insulin-glucose. (Source: eTG Fluids and Electrolytes: Hyperkalaemia)

Cation-exchange resins remove potassium slowly over hours and do not address acute myocardial risk. Their efficacy and safety are also debated (colonic necrosis) and they are not the first step in acute hyperkalaemia with ECG changes. (Source: eTG Fluids and Electrolytes: Hyperkalaemia)

Dialysis is often the definitive treatment for CKD stage 4 with symptomatic hyperkalaemia unresponsive to medical management, but arranging dialysis takes time. Immediate myocardial stabilisation with calcium cannot be deferred. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia)

explanation.summary: Rising lactate 60 minutes after adequate initial crystalloid resuscitation with persistent MAP under 65 mmHg indicates fluid-refractory septic shock. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle then calls for noradrenaline titrated to MAP at least 65 mmHg. Peripheral noradrenaline through a large-bore proximal vein is acceptable as a bridge to central access. Hydrocortisone is added if vasopressor requirement is high (typically noradrenaline >=0.25 microgram/kg/min).
key_points: Hour-1 sepsis bundle: measure lactate, blood cultures before antibiotics, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, vasopressor if MAP <65 after fluid
Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor; peripheral use safe as bridge to central access
MAP target 65 mmHg or above (higher in chronic hypertension may be considered)
Add hydrocortisone 200 mg/day if noradrenaline >=0.25 mcg/kg/min or refractory
explanation.pearls: The 30 mL/kg initial fluid bolus is calculated on actual body weight in most Australian ED protocols; use ideal body weight in class III obesity to avoid over-resuscitation.

options.rationale: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle recommends initial crystalloid 30 mL/kg. Repeat 30 mL/kg fluid boluses beyond the initial resuscitation risk pulmonary oedema without addressing MAP. When MAP <65 after adequate initial fluid, vasopressor initiation is preferred rather than repeated boluses. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

The SSC and ANZICS guidance is to start noradrenaline early when MAP remains under 65 despite adequate initial crystalloid (30 mL/kg). Peripheral noradrenaline infusion through a large-bore proximal vein (antecubital or larger) is now supported for up to 24 hours or bridging to central access, and delays from waiting for central access are associated with worse outcomes. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

Hydrocortisone is added when noradrenaline requirement exceeds 0.25 microgram/kg/min or when shock is refractory. It is not routinely given before vasopressor initiation. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

For community-acquired urosepsis, gentamicin plus amoxicillin-clavulanate provides adequate empiric coverage per Australian Therapeutic Guidelines. Escalation to broader spectrum with MRSA cover is not indicated in this scenario and does not address the immediate perfusion failure. (Source: eTG Antibiotic Urosepsis)

Delaying vasopressor risks prolonged tissue hypoperfusion. MAP target is 65 mmHg or above after initial fluid resuscitation; failure to meet this triggers noradrenaline. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

explanation.summary: Two clinical attacks with objective evidence for at least one and MRI dissemination in space (lesions in at least two typical MS locations) satisfy the 2017 McDonald criteria for relapsing-remitting MS at first neurology contact. CSF-specific oligoclonal bands can substitute for dissemination in time. Acute optic neuritis is treated with IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 to 5 days. Disease-modifying therapy selection is neurologist-led and depends on disease activity, comorbidities and pregnancy plans.
key_points: 2017 McDonald criteria: DIS = lesion in >=2 of 4 typical MS regions (periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial, spinal); DIT = simultaneous asymptomatic + symptomatic lesion or new lesion on follow-up MRI or CSF-specific OCBs
Acute optic neuritis: IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 3-5 days; hastens recovery but does not change final visual outcome (ONTT)
DMT choice ranges from teriflunomide/glatiramer/interferon to natalizumab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, cladribine
Negative AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG plus positive OCBs supports MS over NMOSD/MOGAD
explanation.pearls: The Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial showed IV methylprednisolone accelerates visual recovery in first 2 weeks but does not affect final visual acuity at 12 months; oral prednisone alone showed higher relapse rate.

options.rationale: The prior transient hemibody numbness followed by optic neuritis today represents two clinical attacks in different sites, and MRI demonstrates lesions in more than one typical MS location. Dissemination in space and time is met, so a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis can be made now rather than deferring to CIS. (Source: RACP Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis)

Aquaporin-4 antibody negative, MOG-IgG negative, the MRI pattern (multiple typical MS locations without long spinal cord lesions >=3 vertebral segments), and CSF pattern all favour MS over NMOSD. Rituximab is not first-line without a NMOSD diagnosis. (Source: RACP Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis)

This patient has two clinical attacks (prior hemibody sensory episode plus current optic neuritis) with objective clinical evidence for the current attack (relative afferent pupillary defect, reduced acuity, red desaturation, swollen disc). MRI shows lesions in at least two of the four typical MS locations (periventricular, juxtacortical, cortical, infratentorial, spinal cord), satisfying dissemination in space. CSF-specific oligoclonal bands provide additional support and can substitute for dissemination in time under 2017 criteria. Acute optic neuritis is treated with IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 to 5 days; DMT selection is a neurologist-led decision. (Source: RACP Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis)

MOG-IgG is negative in this patient and the MRI does not show characteristic MOG features (long spinal cord or bilateral optic nerve lesions). Steroid monotherapy alone is not the appropriate long-term approach for MS. (Source: RACP Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis)

Anti-NMDA encephalitis presents with subacute psychiatric symptoms, seizures, movement disorders and autonomic instability rather than optic neuritis with typical MS MRI findings and MS-pattern oligoclonal bands. (Source: RACP Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis)

explanation.summary: High-risk pulmonary embolism (persistent hypotension with right ventricular dysfunction and biomarker elevation) has 30-day mortality of 20 to 30% without reperfusion. Systemic thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours (or 0.6 mg/kg over 15 minutes in cardiac arrest) is the ESC first-line therapy when no absolute contraindications are present. Noradrenaline supports RV perfusion; dobutamine adds inotropy if inotropic failure predominates. Catheter-directed thrombolysis or surgical embolectomy are alternatives in centres where systemic lysis fails or is contraindicated.
key_points: High-risk PE (persistent hypotension + RV dysfunction + elevated biomarkers) requires immediate reperfusion
Systemic alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours is first-line if no absolute contraindication
Absolute contraindications: haemorrhagic stroke ever, ischaemic stroke <6 mo, active bleeding, intracranial neoplasm, recent major surgery or head trauma <3 weeks
Noradrenaline preferred vasopressor in acute RV failure; avoid aggressive fluid loading
explanation.pearls: Alteplase reduced-dose regimen (0.6 mg/kg IV over 15 minutes, max 50 mg) is used during cardiac arrest with suspected PE, per ANZCOR guidance.

options.rationale: In high-risk (haemodynamically unstable) suspected pulmonary embolism where imaging is not immediately available, empiric systemic thrombolysis is recommended after weighing bleeding risk; delaying to await confirmatory imaging risks death from ongoing right ventricular failure. (Source: ANZ Society for Vascular Medicine PE guidance)

There are no clinical features of intracranial haemorrhage. Delaying thrombolysis for a routine CT head in the absence of neurological signs adds mortality. Intubation may further compromise haemodynamics in massive PE due to loss of intrinsic sympathetic drive and worsening venous return. (Source: ANZ Society for Vascular Medicine PE guidance)

Aggressive volume loading in RV failure worsens septal displacement and reduces LV filling further. Small volume challenges (250-500 mL) may be considered, but ionotropic support alone without addressing the clot is insufficient for high-risk PE. (Source: ANZ Society for Vascular Medicine PE guidance)

This is high-risk (massive) pulmonary embolism (sustained hypotension with RV dysfunction and biomarker elevation). ESC and ANZ guidance recommend systemic thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours (or 0.6 mg/kg over 15 minutes up to 50 mg in cardiac arrest) with no absolute contraindications present. Anticoagulation is continued around the infusion per local protocol. Noradrenaline is preferred as vasoactive support in RV failure. (Source: ESC PE Guidelines 2019)

Surgical embolectomy is reserved for patients with absolute contraindications to thrombolysis or failed thrombolysis, and access is limited to specialised centres. It is not first-line when systemic thrombolysis is available and safe. (Source: ESC PE Guidelines 2019)

explanation.summary: Refractory post-STEMI cardiogenic shock (rising lactate, falling MAP despite maximal vasoactive plus inotropic therapy, low mixed venous saturation, oliguria) meets criteria for consideration of VA-ECMO bridge to recovery or decision. IABP alone has no evidence for benefit (IABP-SHOCK II) and has been downgraded. VA-ECMO raises LV afterload; concurrent venting via Impella, IABP or septostomy is standard to prevent pulmonary oedema. ECLS-SHOCK 2023 did not confirm benefit in unselected populations, but selected refractory cases at high-volume centres still receive VA-ECMO.
key_points: IABP in post-STEMI cardiogenic shock: no 30-day, 6-mo, 12-mo mortality benefit (IABP-SHOCK II); ESC downgraded
VA-ECMO for refractory shock: bridge to recovery or decision at high-volume centres despite neutral ECLS-SHOCK results
VA-ECMO raises LV afterload -> concurrent LV vent (Impella, IABP, septostomy) is standard
Australian centres accessed via state ECMO retrieval services
explanation.pearls: SCAI Shock stage E (refractory shock on high-dose vasoactives with rising lactate) has 30-day mortality >75% without MCS in some cohorts; early consultation with ECMO retrieval service improves candidate selection.

options.rationale: IABP-SHOCK II demonstrated no 30-day, 6-month or 12-month mortality benefit for IABP in post-STEMI cardiogenic shock, and current ESC guidelines downgraded IABP for this indication. It is not the correct escalation. (Source: ESC AMI/Cardiogenic Shock 2023)

Escalating vasoactive support in the presence of rising lactate, falling MAP despite maximal doses, and refractory shock will not restore end-organ perfusion; escalation of mechanical support is required. (Source: ESC AMI/Cardiogenic Shock 2023)

Adding an ionodilator in refractory shock at high catecholamine burden with hypotension is unlikely to restore adequate cardiac output and may worsen hypotension; MCS is the required step at this level of refractory shock. (Source: ESC AMI/Cardiogenic Shock 2023)

Haemodialysis does not treat cardiogenic shock. Lactate clearance follows from restored perfusion; dialysis alone does not address the underlying pump failure and delays effective escalation. (Source: ESC AMI/Cardiogenic Shock 2023)

Post-STEMI cardiogenic shock refractory to maximal vasoactive and inotropic support with rising lactate, low mixed venous saturation, oliguria and severe LV dysfunction meets criteria for VA-ECMO bridge to recovery or decision. Australian tertiary centres provide this via ECMO retrieval services (Alfred, RPA, PA). VA-ECMO raises LV afterload and can precipitate pulmonary oedema through LV distension, so a concurrent LV venting strategy (Impella, IABP or atrial septostomy) is standard alongside VA-ECMO. Neither ECLS-SHOCK (2023) nor EURO-SHOCK confirmed mortality benefit in unselected populations, but selected refractory post-STEMI shock at high-volume centres remains an accepted indication. (Source: ESC AMI/Cardiogenic Shock 2023)

explanation.summary: Non-valvular AF stroke prevention is guided by CHA2DS2-VA (Australia dropped the sex category in the 2018 NHFA/CSANZ update, now called CHA2DS2-VA). Score >=2 indicates NOAC therapy: apixaban 5 mg BD (2.5 BD if 2 of age >=80, weight <=60 kg, creatinine >=133), dabigatran 150 mg BD (110 BD if age >=75 or renal impairment), rivaroxaban 20 mg daily (15 mg if CrCl 30 to 49). Warfarin remains first line in mechanical valves and moderate to severe mitral stenosis. Aspirin and dual antiplatelet are not effective substitutes.
key_points: CHA2DS2-VA >=2: NOAC first line in non-valvular AF
Apixaban 5 mg BD; reduce to 2.5 BD if 2 of (age >=80, weight <=60 kg, creatinine >=133)
Warfarin only for mechanical valves or moderate to severe mitral stenosis
Aspirin not recommended for AF stroke prevention
explanation.pearls: For elective procedures on apixaban, hold 24 hours before low bleeding-risk procedures and 48 hours before high bleeding-risk procedures with normal renal function; no bridging with LMWH is required.

options.rationale: Aspirin does not provide adequate stroke prevention in AF and is no longer recommended. It carries bleeding risk without stroke reduction benefit. (Source: NHFA CSANZ AF)

CHA2DS2-VA score is 3 (age 65 to 74 = 1, HTN = 1, DM = 1) indicating clear anticoagulation benefit. NOAC (apixaban, dabigatran, rivaroxaban) is first choice over warfarin in non-valvular AF. Apixaban 5 mg BD is standard unless dose reduction criteria (age >=80, weight <=60 kg, creatinine >=133 umol/L, with at least 2 of 3) are met. (Source: NHFA CSANZ AF)
CHA2DS2-VA of 3 confers an annual stroke risk of approximately 3.2 percent; anticoagulation reduces this substantially and is clearly indicated. (Source: NHFA CSANZ AF)

Warfarin is second choice in non-valvular AF; NOACs are preferred for equivalent or superior efficacy, lower intracranial haemorrhage risk, and no INR monitoring. Warfarin remains first choice in mechanical valves and moderate to severe mitral stenosis. (Source: NHFA CSANZ AF)
Dual antiplatelet therapy is inferior to anticoagulation for stroke prevention in AF and carries substantial bleeding risk. It is not a substitute for anticoagulation. (Source: NHFA CSANZ AF)

explanation.summary: Acute ischaemic stroke reperfusion combines IV alteplase (within 4.5 hours; tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg is now guideline-endorsed as equivalent or superior in Australia) with endovascular thrombectomy for anterior circulation large vessel occlusion (within 6 hours routinely, up to 24 hours with favourable perfusion imaging). BP is treated to <185/110 before alteplase. Contraindications include haemorrhage, recent major surgery, prior intracerebral haemorrhage, active bleeding, INR >1.7 or NOAC use within window, platelets <100.
key_points: IV alteplase 0.9 mg/kg within 4.5 hours (tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg equivalent in Australia)
Endovascular thrombectomy for anterior circulation LVO up to 6 hours (24 hours with imaging)
BP target <185/110 before thrombolysis; <180/105 during and 24 hours after
Aspirin use is NOT a contraindication to alteplase
explanation.pearls: Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg as single IV bolus has replaced alteplase in many Australian stroke units; it is faster to administer (single bolus vs 60 minute infusion), does not delay transfer for thrombectomy, and shows equivalent or better outcomes in AcT and EXTEND-IA TNK trials.

options.rationale: Delaying thrombectomy in a patient with proximal LVO within the treatment window costs salvageable brain. Aspirin is not a substitute for thrombolysis or thrombectomy when both are indicated. (Source: Stroke Foundation)
Target BP before alteplase is <185/110, not <140/80. Aggressive BP lowering can worsen infarct extension by reducing collateral flow. (Source: Stroke Foundation)

Within 4.5 hours of witnessed onset and no contraindications, IV alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg, 10 percent as bolus over 1 minute, remainder over 60 minutes) is standard. Proximal M1 occlusion with NIHSS 12 and imaging showing salvageable brain warrants concurrent endovascular thrombectomy (up to 6 hours from onset routinely; up to 24 hours with perfusion imaging showing mismatch). BP is treated to <185/110 before alteplase. (Source: Stroke Foundation)
Early therapeutic anticoagulation is not beneficial and increases haemorrhage risk. Alteplase and thrombectomy are the reperfusion strategies. (Source: Stroke Foundation)
Aspirin use is not a contraindication to alteplase. Nimodipine is for subarachnoid haemorrhage vasospasm, not ischaemic stroke. (Source: Stroke Foundation)

explanation.summary: Acute severe asthma is treated with continuous or back-to-back nebulised salbutamol 5 mg (or MDI plus spacer 4 to 12 puffs) with ipratropium 500 mcg added for severe exacerbations, controlled oxygen to target SpO2 93 to 95 percent (avoid hyperoxia), and systemic corticosteroid (prednisolone 50 mg oral or hydrocortisone 100 mg IV) within 1 hour. IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes is added if no rapid improvement. Life-threatening features (silent chest, cyanosis, bradycardia, exhaustion, altered LOC, PEF <33 percent) prompt ICU escalation and consideration of intubation.
key_points: Salbutamol 5 mg + ipratropium 500 mcg nebulised, controlled O2 to SpO2 93 to 95 percent
Prednisolone 50 mg oral (or hydrocortisone 100 mg IV) within 1 hour
IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 min if no rapid improvement
ICU review for life-threatening features (silent chest, exhaustion, altered LOC, PEF <33 percent)
explanation.pearls: Discharge criteria after acute asthma: PEF >=75 percent predicted or personal best, stable on 4-hourly bronchodilator, review of technique and adherence, prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 to 7 days total, written action plan, and follow-up within 2 to 7 days.

options.rationale: NIV in acute asthma has limited evidence and can worsen air trapping and hyperinflation. Bronchodilator therapy, oxygen, and steroids are first line. Intubation is considered for exhaustion or CO2 rise. (Source: NAC AAMH)

Antibiotics are not routinely indicated unless there is evidence of bacterial infection. Discharge is unsafe in acute severe asthma; the patient requires immediate escalated bronchodilator therapy and steroids. (Source: NAC AAMH)
Theophylline is not first line and has a narrow therapeutic index. Nebulised salbutamol plus ipratropium, oxygen, and systemic corticosteroid are the first-line management. (Source: NAC AAMH)

Acute severe asthma (unable to complete sentences, RR >=25, HR >=110, SpO2 <92 percent, PEF 33 to 50 percent) is treated with continuous or back-to-back nebulised salbutamol plus ipratropium, controlled oxygen to target SpO2 93 to 95 percent, oral prednisolone 50 mg (or IV hydrocortisone 100 mg if oral not tolerated), and IV magnesium sulfate 2 g if no rapid improvement. (Source: NAC AAMH)
IM adrenaline is reserved for anaphylaxis or life-threatening asthma with imminent arrest. It is not first line in acute severe asthma when nebulised salbutamol can be delivered. (Source: NAC AAMH)

explanation.summary: In type 2 diabetes with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease, an SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) or GLP-1 receptor agonist (semaglutide, dulaglutide, liraglutide) with proven cardiovascular or renal benefit is added regardless of HbA1c. SGLT2 inhibitors are preferred in heart failure and CKD; GLP-1 RA give greater HbA1c and weight reduction. Both reduce major adverse cardiovascular events. Sulfonylureas, DPP-4 inhibitors, and insulin remain useful for glycaemic control without cardioprotective benefit.
key_points: T2DM + ASCVD: add SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA regardless of HbA1c
SGLT2i preferred in heart failure and CKD (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin)
GLP-1 RA give greater HbA1c and weight reduction (semaglutide, dulaglutide)
Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycaemia and weight gain, no CV benefit
explanation.pearls: SGLT2 inhibitor sick day rules: withhold during acute illness, dehydration, fasting, and surgery to reduce euglycaemic DKA risk. Warn about mycotic genital infections (approximately 5 to 10 percent, more in women) and rare Fournier's gangrene.

options.rationale: Sulfonylureas do not provide cardiovascular benefit and carry hypoglycaemia and weight gain risks. In a patient with established ASCVD, SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA is preferred as second line. (Source: RACGP Diabetes)

Insulin is added when other options have failed or in specific circumstances (severe hyperglycaemia, symptomatic). It causes hypoglycaemia and weight gain without cardiovascular benefit. Cardioprotective agent first. (Source: RACGP Diabetes)
Pioglitazone carries risks of heart failure, weight gain, fractures, and bladder cancer signal. It is not preferred over SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA in patients with ASCVD. (Source: RACGP Diabetes)
DPP-4 inhibitors are weight neutral with low hypoglycaemia but do not provide cardiovascular protection. In ASCVD, SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA is preferred as second line. (Source: RACGP Diabetes)

In T2DM with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, an SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) or GLP-1 receptor agonist (semaglutide, dulaglutide, liraglutide) with proven cardiovascular benefit is added regardless of HbA1c. Empagliflozin reduces cardiovascular death, MI, stroke, and heart failure hospitalisation (EMPA-REG). (Source: RACGP Diabetes)

explanation.summary: Preoperative preparation for pheochromocytoma requires alpha blockade before beta blockade to prevent hypertensive crisis from unopposed alpha stimulation during tumour manipulation. Phenoxybenzamine is the standard non-selective alpha blocker, started at 10 mg twice daily and titrated up. Adequate blockade is achieved with target seated BP below 130/80, standing BP above 90 systolic, mild orthostatic drop, and Hb rise reflecting plasma volume expansion. Beta blockade is added only if reflex tachycardia develops.
key_points: Alpha blockade FIRST (phenoxybenzamine 10 to 14 days minimum)
Beta blockade ONLY after alpha blockade if tachycardia
Liberal salt intake to counter volume contraction
Intraoperative watch for BP swings and post-resection hypotension
explanation.pearls: Roizen criteria for adequate alpha blockade: seated BP <130/80, standing SBP >90, mild orthostasis, no ECG ST-T changes for 2 weeks; phenoxybenzamine typical dose 20 to 100 mg/day divided doses.

options.rationale: Magnesium infusion is used intraoperatively as an adjunct; it is not the standard preoperative preparation, which is oral alpha blockade over 10 to 14 days plus salt loading. (Source: eTG Endocrinology)
Starting beta blockade before alpha blockade leaves alpha1 vasoconstriction unopposed, precipitating hypertensive crisis; alpha blockade must come first. (Source: eTG Endocrinology)

ACE inhibitors and calcium channel blockers are not the preferred first-line preoperative preparation because they do not blunt catecholamine surges during tumour manipulation. Alpha blockade is the standard. (Source: eTG Endocrinology)

Operating without preoperative alpha blockade causes intraoperative hypertensive crisis from catecholamine release with high risk of stroke, myocardial infarction and death. (Source: eTG Endocrinology)

Non-selective alpha blockade (phenoxybenzamine) for a minimum of 10 to 14 days before surgery is standard; beta blockade may be added only AFTER adequate alpha blockade to control reflex tachycardia. Beta blockade first would leave unopposed alpha stimulation and can precipitate hypertensive crisis. (Source: eTG Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Guillain-Barré syndrome is an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy typically preceded by a diarrhoeal or respiratory illness. It causes ascending symmetric weakness with areflexia and albuminocytological CSF dissociation. Respiratory failure is the main killer; regular FVC and NIF are required, with intubation if FVC below 20 mL/kg (roughly 1 litre for average adults) or NIF above minus 25 cmH2O or rapid decline. Treatment is IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days or 5-session plasma exchange, both equally effective.
key_points: IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day x 5 days OR plasma exchange, NOT both
FVC less than 20 mL/kg (~1 L) or NIF less than -25 cmH2O equals ICU intubation
Steroids alone are NOT effective
VTE prophylaxis with LMWH, autonomic monitoring for dysrhythmia and BP swings
explanation.pearls: 20/30/40 rule for respiratory triage: FVC <20 mL/kg, NIF <-30, or MEP <40 cmH2O predict need for mechanical ventilation. Serial 4-hourly bedside spirometry in first 48 hours.

options.rationale: Guillain-Barré syndrome with FVC 40 percent predicted and weak cough warrants monitored admission, prompt IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days (equivalent efficacy to plasma exchange but easier logistically), and clear ICU triggers for intubation before crisis. (Source: eTG Neurology)
Corticosteroids alone are ineffective in Guillain-Barré syndrome and delay definitive treatment; IVIG or plasma exchange is standard. (Source: eTG Neurology)
FVC 40 percent predicted with weak cough is a red flag for impending respiratory failure; outpatient management is unsafe until progression has clearly plateaued. (Source: eTG Neurology)
Combined IVIG plus plasma exchange offers no benefit over either alone and adds cost and risk; choose one modality. Blanket ICU admission without triggers is not the standard. (Source: eTG Neurology)

Cord compression is unlikely given areflexia, facial weakness, and albuminocytological dissociation on CSF; delaying treatment for MRI is inappropriate although imaging may still be arranged in parallel if red flags exist. (Source: eTG Neurology)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection is classified as Stanford type A (ascending, requires urgent surgery) or type B (descending, medical unless malperfusion). Immediate management is aggressive control of heart rate then blood pressure to reduce aortic wall shear stress: beta blocker infusion (esmolol or labetalol) targeting heart rate 60, then vasodilator (nitroprusside or GTN) for BP 100 to 120 systolic. Type A patients need emergency cardiothoracic surgical repair. Pericardiocentesis for tamponade is avoided outside theatre.
key_points: Type A (ascending) equals emergency surgery; type B (descending) usually medical
Heart rate control (beta blocker) FIRST to reduce dP/dt, then BP control
Target HR 60, SBP 100 to 120
Avoid pericardiocentesis in type A with effusion (bleeding risk)
explanation.pearls: Untreated Stanford type A dissection mortality: 1 to 2 percent per hour in the first 48 hours; 50 percent by 48 hours. IRAD registry confirms surgery reduces in-hospital mortality from 58 percent (medical) to 27 percent (surgical).

options.rationale: Antiplatelet and anticoagulant loading is contraindicated in dissection because they increase haemorrhage risk; treatment is surgical, not ACS-directed. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular)

Nitroprusside before beta blockade causes reflex tachycardia that worsens shear stress and dissection propagation; beta blockade must come first. Endovascular repair is for type B dissection, not type A. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular)

Type A (ascending) aortic dissection requires urgent surgical repair; medical therapy targets heart rate 60 and SBP 100 to 120 (beta blocker FIRST to reduce dP/dt then vasodilator if needed) while arranging immediate transfer. Untreated Stanford type A has 1 to 2 percent per hour mortality. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular)

Ward-level observation is inadequate for type A dissection; delayed surgery increases mortality by 1 to 2 percent per hour, so immediate cardiothoracic transfer is required. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular)

Pericardiocentesis is contraindicated in dissection with pericardial effusion because decompression can restart bleeding into the pericardium and precipitate death; drain in theatre only if in tamponade arrest during surgery. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Sympathetic crashing acute pulmonary oedema (SCAPE) is a hypertensive emergency with acute afterload mismatch and flash pulmonary oedema. First-line treatment is non-invasive positive pressure ventilation, IV nitrate (GTN infusion), and diuresis. Target 20 to 25 percent reduction in mean arterial pressure over the first hour, then further gradual reduction. Morphine is avoided because of mortality signal. Rapid supra-physiological reduction risks stroke and organ ischaemia.
key_points: SCAPE (hypertensive APO): NIV + IV GTN + IV diuretic
Target MAP fall 20 to 25% in first hour, NOT rapid to normal
Morphine avoided (mortality signal)
Intubation only if NIV fails or altered consciousness
explanation.pearls: IV GTN dose in SCAPE: start 5 to 10 mcg/min, uptitrate every 3 to 5 min to effect (up to 200 mcg/min). Rapid afterload reduction resolves oedema within 30 to 60 min in most cases.

options.rationale: Oral therapy is too slow for hypertensive pulmonary oedema; IV afterload reduction with GTN and IV furosemide is required alongside non-invasive ventilation. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular)

Rapid target BP below 140 within 30 minutes risks under-perfusion of vital organs; the standard target is 20 to 25 percent MAP reduction in the first hour. GTN is preferred over labetalol in acute pulmonary oedema because beta blockade may worsen decompensated failure. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular)

Morphine in acute pulmonary oedema is associated with increased mortality and does not treat the underlying hypertensive afterload; troponin rise here is demand-related and does not indicate acute plaque rupture. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular)

Hypertensive acute pulmonary oedema (SCAPE) responds to non-invasive positive pressure ventilation to reduce work of breathing and afterload, IV GTN as first-line afterload reduction (target MAP fall 20 to 25 percent in the first hour), and diuresis. This addresses both blood pressure and pulmonary oedema. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular)

Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation is first-line and often avoids intubation in SCAPE; intubation should be reserved for NIV failure, exhaustion, or altered consciousness. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Empiric therapy for adult community-acquired bacterial meningitis is IV ceftriaxone 2 g plus IV benzylpenicillin 2.4 g (Listeria cover for age 50 or older, immunocompromised, pregnant, alcohol use disorder). Dexamethasone 10 mg IV 6-hourly is given with or just before the first antibiotic dose because it reduces mortality and hearing loss in pneumococcal meningitis. LP should not delay antibiotics; CT before LP is required if depressed consciousness, focal deficit, seizure, immunocompromised, or papilloedema.
key_points: Blood cultures first, then dex 10 mg IV, then ceftriaxone 2 g + benzylpenicillin 2.4 g
Benzylpenicillin adds Listeria cover for age >=50, immunocompromised, chronic illness
Do not delay antibiotics for LP or CT
CT before LP if reduced GCS, focal signs, seizure, immunocompromised, papilloedema
explanation.pearls: Aciclovir 10 mg/kg IV 8-hourly added if encephalitis features (focal deficit, seizure, personality change). Contact precautions and PEP for close contacts of confirmed meningococcal disease (ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO single dose).

options.rationale: The picture is classic bacterial meningitis (petechiae, neck stiffness, rapid onset); HSV encephalitis presents with focal deficit, seizure, or personality change. Aciclovir may be added if encephalitis is suspected but is not the first single agent. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

Antibiotics must not be delayed for LP in suspected bacterial meningitis; blood cultures first, then empiric antibiotics with dexamethasone, and LP as soon as safe. CSF culture yield is reduced by pre-LP antibiotics but the risk of delaying treatment far outweighs this. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

Ceftriaxone does not cover Listeria monocytogenes; adults 50 years and older, immunocompromised, or with chronic illness need added benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin for Listeria empirically. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

Dexamethasone must be given with or just before the first antibiotic dose to be effective; deferring it until culture results loses the survival and hearing preservation benefit shown in pneumococcal meningitis. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

Adult community-acquired bacterial meningitis is treated with empiric IV ceftriaxone plus benzylpenicillin (for Listeria cover if over 50 years) after blood cultures; dexamethasone 10 mg IV is given just before or with the first antibiotic dose to reduce hearing loss and mortality in pneumococcal meningitis. LP follows if not contraindicated. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Chronic corticosteroid therapy at doses of 5 mg prednisolone or higher for more than 3 to 4 weeks suppresses the HPA axis and predisposes to adrenal crisis under stress (sepsis, surgery, trauma). Empirical hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus then 200 mg over 24 hours by infusion (or 50 mg IV 6-hourly) is life-saving and given before diagnostic testing. Classical biochemistry includes hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, and hypotension refractory to fluid alone.
key_points: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus then 200 mg/24 h infusion (or 50 mg IV 6h)
Treat empirically; do NOT delay for synacthen test
Hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia + hypoglycaemia + shock triad
Long-term on 5+ mg prednisolone requires stress-dose steroid education
explanation.pearls: All patients on prednisolone 5 mg/day for >4 weeks need MedicAlert and stress dose plan: double oral steroid for minor illness, hydrocortisone 100 mg IM (Emerpen or SoluCortef) for vomiting or surgery.

options.rationale: Oral steroids are inadequate for adrenal crisis in a shocked, drowsy patient with likely absorption compromise; parenteral hydrocortisone is required immediately. (Source: eTG Endocrinology)

Chronic prednisolone at 7.5 mg for years suppresses the HPA axis; septic shock is a major physiological stressor causing adrenal crisis. IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg/24 h (or 50 mg 6-hourly) is empirical and life-saving; hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia support the diagnosis. (Source: eTG Endocrinology)

Diagnostic testing must not delay steroid replacement in suspected adrenal crisis; treat empirically, test later once stabilised (and note that recent hydrocortisone will affect cortisol assay). (Source: eTG Endocrinology)
Fludrocortisone has slow onset and is not standard acute therapy for adrenal crisis; hydrocortisone at stress doses provides sufficient mineralocorticoid activity acutely. (Source: eTG Endocrinology)
Withholding stress-dose hydrocortisone in adrenal crisis is fatal; the benefit far outweighs any additional infection risk, and antibiotics address the sepsis in parallel. (Source: eTG Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a rapidly progressive soft tissue infection with high mortality if surgery is delayed. Clinical clues include pain out of proportion, dusky or bullous skin change, crepitus, and systemic sepsis. LRINEC score of 6 or more raises suspicion; 8 or more is high risk. Immediate management is aggressive resuscitation, empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics including clindamycin for toxin suppression, and urgent surgical debridement in theatre. Imaging must not delay theatre.
key_points: Surgical debridement is the primary and time-critical intervention
Empiric: meropenem + vancomycin + clindamycin (toxin suppression)
LRINEC score >=6 raises suspicion; clinical judgement outranks the score
Do NOT delay theatre for MRI in a septic patient with classic features
explanation.pearls: LRINEC variables: CRP, WCC, Hb, sodium, creatinine, glucose. Score >=8 has PPV around 90% for NF; however sensitivity is imperfect so a lower score does not exclude the diagnosis clinically.

options.rationale: Necrotising fasciitis (LRINEC 9 with pain out of proportion, crepitus, and haemorrhagic bullae) is a surgical emergency; source control by wide debridement in theatre is the definitive treatment and must not be delayed for imaging. Empiric broad-spectrum plus clindamycin (for toxin suppression) is standard. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

Imaging must not delay operative debridement in high-probability necrotising fasciitis; MRI or CT may be used only when the diagnosis is uncertain and clinical picture allows. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

Flucloxacillin monotherapy is inadequate for necrotising fasciitis, which is often polymicrobial or streptococcal with toxin production; treating this as cellulitis loses the surgical window. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)
Hyperbaric oxygen has an unproven role and should not delay surgical source control; vancomycin alone lacks Gram-negative and anaerobic cover. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)
Bedside biopsy is not standard and delays definitive theatre debridement; the clinical picture and LRINEC score are sufficient to proceed. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Acute gout in CKD is treated with oral or intra-articular corticosteroid as first-line because NSAIDs are contraindicated and colchicine accumulates. Oral prednisolone 25 to 30 mg for 3 to 5 days is effective and generally well tolerated. Urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol) is initiated after the acute flare settles, starting at low dose (50 mg in eGFR under 30) and uptitrated to a serum urate target of 0.36 mmol/L (or 0.30 with tophi), with colchicine or NSAID cover as flare prophylaxis where safe.
key_points: NSAIDs contraindicated in CKD; colchicine accumulates in eGFR <30
Oral prednisolone 25 to 30 mg for 3 to 5 days is first-line in CKD
Allopurinol start dose in eGFR <30: 50 mg, titrate every 4 weeks
Target serum urate <0.36 mmol/L (<0.30 with tophi)
explanation.pearls: HLA-B*5801 screening pre-allopurinol reduces SJS/TEN risk (particularly Han Chinese, Korean, Thai populations). Febuxostat is an alternative XO inhibitor but has cardiovascular safety concerns and is second-line.

options.rationale: NSAIDs are contraindicated in stage 4 CKD because of the risk of further renal impairment and hyperkalaemia; steroids or intra-articular therapy are safer alternatives. (Source: eTG Rheumatology)

In stage 4 CKD, NSAIDs are contraindicated and colchicine risks accumulation and toxicity; oral prednisolone 25 to 30 mg daily for 3 to 5 days is a preferred first-line acute anti-inflammatory choice in CKD. Urate-lowering therapy is discussed after the acute flare with allopurinol started low and titrated. (Source: eTG Rheumatology)

Colchicine accumulates in stage 4 CKD (eGFR under 30) with high toxicity risk (neuromyopathy, cytopenias); dose reduction to 500 micrograms daily is possible but steroid is generally preferred. (Source: eTG Rheumatology)

Starting allopurinol during an acute flare can prolong or worsen it; also 300 mg is too high a start dose in stage 4 CKD (start 50 mg and titrate). Urate-lowering therapy is discussed after the flare settles. (Source: eTG Rheumatology)

Intra-articular steroid is reasonable for a single joint when infection is excluded, but oral prednisolone is simpler and equally effective in this context; aspirating a first MTP is technically difficult and injection risks contamination. (Source: eTG Rheumatology)

explanation.summary: Massive (high risk) pulmonary embolism is defined by sustained hypotension or shock from acute PE. Systemic thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours plus concurrent unfractionated heparin is first line when there are no absolute bleeding contraindications. Surgical embolectomy or catheter directed thrombolysis are reserved for failed or contraindicated systemic tPA. Anticoagulation alone or IVC filter placement do not treat the obstruction.
key_points: Massive PE: shock or hypotension plus PE, immediate reperfusion needed
Alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours plus UFH infusion is first line
Surgical embolectomy or CDT if tPA fails or contraindicated
IVC filter only when anticoagulation is contraindicated
explanation.pearls: PE mortality with shock is around 30 to 50 percent untreated and falls to 10 to 20 percent with prompt tPA; alteplase 0.6 mg per kg over 15 minutes bolus is used in cardiac arrest from suspected PE, standard 100 mg over 2 hours in sustained shock without arrest.

sources.label: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement

options.rationale: Catheter directed thrombolysis is considered for submassive PE where bleeding risk from full dose systemic tPA is high; in massive PE with shock, systemic tPA is faster and first line. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement

options.rationale: Anticoagulation alone does not reperfuse and is insufficient in massive PE with obstructive shock; reperfusion by thrombolysis or embolectomy is required. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement

options.rationale: Surgical embolectomy is second line if thrombolysis fails or is contraindicated; first line for massive PE without contraindication is systemic tPA. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement

options.rationale: Massive PE with sustained hypotension and RV dysfunction is a class I indication for systemic thrombolysis with alteplase; concurrent unfractionated heparin is titrated to APTT after tPA. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement

options.rationale: IVC filters do not treat the existing clot causing shock and delaying tPA is dangerous in massive PE; filters are reserved for anticoagulation contraindication or recurrence on therapy. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement

explanation.summary: Severe DKA with initial potassium under 3.3 mmol/L is a contraindication to starting insulin because insulin drives potassium intracellularly and precipitates arrhythmia. The priority is fluid resuscitation and potassium replacement to above 3.5 mmol/L before commencing IV insulin infusion at 0.1 units per kg per hour. Bicarbonate is not routine even at pH under 7.00. Add dextrose when glucose falls under 14 mmol/L on insulin infusion.
key_points: Potassium under 3.3 mmol/L: hold insulin until corrected to above 3.5
Standard fixed rate insulin: 0.1 units per kg per hour IV
Bicarbonate not routinely indicated in DKA even at pH under 7.00
Add dextrose 10 percent when glucose falls under 14 mmol/L on insulin
explanation.pearls: ADS thresholds: hold insulin K under 3.3, add KCl 40 mmol per litre if K 3.3 to 5.3; cerebral oedema risk in adults is low but reduce fluid rate if child, symptoms occur usually 4 to 12 hours in, treat with mannitol 0.5 to 1 g per kg or 3 percent saline 5 mL per kg.

options.rationale: Dextrose is added when glucose falls under 14 mmol/L on insulin, not initially at glucose 32; and insulin cannot start until K over 3.3 mmol/L is corrected. (Source: ADS DKA Guideline)
Starting insulin with potassium under 3.3 mmol/L causes dangerous intracellular potassium shift and arrhythmia; correct K to 3.5 first. (Source: ADS DKA Guideline)

Bicarbonate does not improve outcomes in DKA and can worsen hypokalaemia and cerebral oedema risk; it is not routinely indicated even at pH under 7.00 unless refractory shock is present. (Source: ADS DKA Guideline)
SC insulin is unreliable in shock or dehydration and is not first line in severe DKA; IV infusion is standard, and hypokalaemia must be corrected before starting insulin. (Source: ADS DKA Guideline)

Potassium under 3.3 mmol/L is a contraindication to starting insulin because insulin drives further intracellular shift and precipitates arrhythmia; correct K first, then start insulin at 0.1 units per kg per hour. (Source: ADS DKA Guideline)
