explanation.summary: Acute ischaemic stroke with a disabling deficit and confirmed anterior circulation large vessel occlusion should receive IV thrombolysis within 4.5 hours if no contraindication, plus endovascular thrombectomy up to 24 hours with favourable imaging. Tenecteplase 0.25 mg per kg has non-inferior evidence to alteplase and is now often first line in Australia. Combined therapy is better than either alone.
key_points: IV tenecteplase 0.25 mg per kg within 4.5 hours of onset for eligible patients
Endovascular thrombectomy for anterior circulation LVO up to 24 hours with mismatch
Antiplatelet use is not a contraindication to IV thrombolysis
Blood pressure target under 185/110 before tPA, under 180/105 for 24 hours after
explanation.pearls: Australian Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines now recommend tenecteplase 0.25 mg per kg IV single bolus as an alternative to alteplase within 4.5 hours; thrombectomy has NNT around 4 to 5 for functional independence in LVO stroke within 6 hours.

options.rationale: Within 4.5 hours of onset with no contraindication, IV thrombolysis (tenecteplase or alteplase) plus endovascular thrombectomy for a large vessel occlusion is first line and outperforms either alone. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines Australia)

Antiplatelet use is not a contraindication to IV thrombolysis; skipping tPA loses the benefit of pre-thrombectomy reperfusion and small vessel clot clearance. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines Australia)

Large vessel occlusion with disabling deficit benefits from thrombectomy even after tPA; withholding it wastes proven mortality and functional benefit. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines Australia)
Dual antiplatelet loading is not reperfusion and is not appropriate as sole therapy in disabling stroke with LVO within the reperfusion window. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines Australia)
Delay of reperfusion loses time-dependent benefit; the mismatch profile at 4 hours already supports urgent tPA plus thrombectomy. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines Australia)

explanation.summary: Refractory cardiogenic shock after STEMI with escalating vasopressor need and rising lactate is an indication for mechanical circulatory support, with recent evidence (DanGer Shock 2024) supporting Impella CP over IABP or medical therapy alone in selected STEMI shock. IABP has no mortality benefit. Adding more inotropes or preload reducers can worsen outcomes. Early escalation before multi-organ failure is key.
key_points: Refractory STEMI cardiogenic shock: escalate to mechanical support early
DanGer Shock trial: Impella CP mortality benefit in STEMI shock
IABP-SHOCK II: no mortality benefit for IABP in post-MI shock
Avoid vasodilators like GTN when SBP under 90 mmHg
explanation.pearls: DanGer Shock 2024 NEJM showed 6 month mortality 45.8 percent Impella CP vs 58.5 percent standard care in STEMI shock, at cost of more bleeding and limb ischaemia; VA-ECMO used when biventricular failure or Impella insufficient.

sources.label: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement

options.rationale: Adding an inotrope on top of high dose vasopressor in worsening shock is unlikely to reverse hypoperfusion and delays escalation to mechanical support with proven benefit. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement

options.rationale: In cardiogenic shock after STEMI unresponsive to inotropes with escalating lactate, mechanical circulatory support (Impella or VA-ECMO in some centres) is indicated; the DanGer Shock trial showed Impella CP mortality benefit in selected STEMI shock. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement

options.rationale: Glyceryl trinitrate lowers preload and can precipitate profound hypotension in cardiogenic shock with SBP under 90; it is inappropriate as an escalation step here. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement

options.rationale: Levosimendan can worsen hypotension in fixed cardiogenic shock and has not shown mortality benefit; it is not the priority when mechanical support is available. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement

options.rationale: IABP-SHOCK II showed no mortality benefit for IABP in post-MI cardiogenic shock; contemporary practice favours Impella or VA-ECMO for refractory shock. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement

explanation.summary: Severe or near-fatal asthma with exhaustion, silent chest, and rising CO2 despite maximal medical therapy requires intubation. Ketamine is the preferred induction agent for its bronchodilator effect. Post-intubation ventilation uses low tidal volumes, low rate, long expiratory time, and permissive hypercapnia to avoid dynamic hyperinflation. NIV is not first line in this deteriorating scenario.
key_points: Life threatening asthma with rising CO2 or silent chest: intubate
Ketamine 1 to 2 mg per kg IV is preferred induction agent
Permissive hypercapnia and prolonged expiratory time post intubation
Watch for dynamic hyperinflation and pneumothorax during ventilation
explanation.pearls: TSANZ suggests tidal volume 5 to 6 mL per kg, RR 8 to 10, I:E 1:4, plateau pressure under 30, allow pCO2 up to 80 mmHg with pH over 7.15; ketamine dose 1 to 2 mg per kg IV, with rocuronium 1.2 mg per kg for RSI.

options.rationale: Aminophylline has limited additional benefit over maximal beta-agonist plus magnesium and adds arrhythmia risk in a patient already needing intubation. (Source: TSANZ/ANZSA Severe Asthma Guideline)

NIV in severe asthma with silent chest, exhaustion, and rising CO2 delays definitive airway and risks arrest; intubation is indicated now, not further NIV. (Source: TSANZ/ANZSA Severe Asthma Guideline)

Life threatening asthma with rising CO2 and exhaustion after maximal therapy requires intubation; ketamine is preferred induction agent for bronchodilator effect and cardiovascular stability, with permissive hypercapnia thereafter. (Source: TSANZ/ANZSA Severe Asthma Guideline)
Repeating magnesium is not evidence supported and steroid effect takes hours; the patient needs an airway now, not another delayed pharmacological trial. (Source: TSANZ/ANZSA Severe Asthma Guideline)

Systemic adrenaline is reserved for peri-arrest anaphylaxis or shock; it does not replace intubation in exhausted asthma with rising CO2 and silent chest. (Source: TSANZ/ANZSA Severe Asthma Guideline)

explanation.summary: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizure or reduced GCS is treated with 150 mL 3 percent saline IV over 10 minutes, repeated once or twice, targeting a rise of 4 to 6 mmol/L to abort cerebral symptoms, then capped at 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome. Isotonic saline can worsen the picture in SIAD-type physiology. Tolvaptan and free water restriction are for chronic settings.
key_points: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia: 150 mL 3% saline bolus over 10 minutes
Repeat once or twice to raise Na 4 to 6 mmol/L to abort symptoms
Cap correction at 8 to 10 mmol/L per 24 hours to prevent ODS
Do not use tolvaptan in acute symptomatic phase
explanation.pearls: European guideline (2014) and Aussie NKF: 150 mL 3% saline IV over 10 minutes as bolus; if over-correction occurs, give 5% dextrose 10 mL per kg over 1 hour plus DDAVP 2 to 4 mcg subcut to reverse.

options.rationale: Tolvaptan risks over-rapid correction and osmotic demyelination and is not first line in acute symptomatic severe hyponatraemia; hypertonic saline in controlled boluses is standard. (Source: European Hyponatraemia Guideline)

Isotonic saline can worsen hyponatraemia by adding to intake in SIAD physiology; symptomatic severe hyponatraemia needs hypertonic saline, not isotonic infusion, to raise sodium quickly. (Source: European Hyponatraemia Guideline)
Fluid restriction alone is far too slow for a patient with active seizure and Na 110; hypertonic saline is needed to stop cerebral symptoms rapidly. (Source: European Hyponatraemia Guideline)

Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizure, coma) is treated with hypertonic saline boluses to raise sodium by 4 to 6 mmol/L rapidly to stop symptoms, capped at 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination. (Source: European Hyponatraemia Guideline)

Furosemide plus isotonic saline can be used cautiously in some volume overload chronic cases but is inappropriate in acute symptomatic severe hyponatraemia; hypertonic bolus stops cerebral symptoms fastest. (Source: European Hyponatraemia Guideline)

explanation.summary: TB meningitis is treated with a 2 month intensive phase of rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, then a 7 to 10 month continuation phase of rifampicin and isoniazid, alongside adjunctive dexamethasone tapered over 6 to 8 weeks. Steroids reduce mortality by around 30 percent. CSF classically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, high protein, very low glucose, and high opening pressure. GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra on CSF is the first-line rapid test.
key_points: TBM treatment: 2 months RIPE plus 7 to 10 months RH, with dexamethasone taper
Dexamethasone reduces mortality across HIV-negative and HIV-positive adults
CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis, protein over 1 g/L, glucose under 40% serum
GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra on CSF is preferred rapid diagnostic
explanation.pearls: Thwaites steroid regimen: dexamethasone 0.4 mg per kg per day IV for 1 week, 0.3 for week 2, 0.2 for week 3, 0.1 for week 4, then 4 mg orally reducing over 4 weeks; add pyridoxine 25 mg daily with isoniazid to prevent neuropathy.

options.rationale: Two-drug induction is inadequate for TB meningitis and risks resistance and treatment failure; standard four-drug induction with steroids is indicated even before sputum results. (Source: WHO TB Consolidated Guidelines)

Bacterial meningitis cover alone misses TB, and the CSF profile (lymphocytic pleocytosis, very low glucose, high protein, opening pressure 32) is classic for TB, especially with positive GeneXpert pending. (Source: WHO TB Consolidated Guidelines)

HSV encephalitis produces temporal lobe changes and PCR-positive CSF, not basal meningeal enhancement with markedly low glucose; aciclovir alone misses the treatable TB. (Source: WHO TB Consolidated Guidelines)
Adjunctive dexamethasone reduces mortality in TB meningitis and is standard alongside RIPE; withholding steroids loses a proven mortality benefit. (Source: WHO TB Consolidated Guidelines)

TB meningitis is treated with standard RIPE quadruple therapy plus adjunctive dexamethasone (Thwaites regimen), which reduces mortality across HIV-negative and HIV-positive adults. (Source: WHO TB Consolidated Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Refractory anaphylaxis after two doses of IM adrenaline needs escalation to an IV adrenaline infusion. In patients on beta-blockers who fail to respond, IV glucagon 1 to 5 mg bolus can bypass the beta-block via cAMP. Adjunctive steroids and antihistamines do not treat shock. Airway must be secured urgently if stridor is worsening.
key_points: Refractory anaphylaxis: escalate to IV adrenaline infusion
IV glucagon 1 to 5 mg for beta-blocker refractoriness
Adrenaline is first line, noradrenaline second line adjunct
Steroids and antihistamines are adjunctive, not shock therapy
explanation.pearls: ANZAAG lists IV adrenaline 1 mg in 1000 mL saline = 1 mcg per mL, start at 5 mL per minute in an adult; glucagon 1 to 5 mg IV bolus over 5 minutes for beta-blocker refractoriness, may repeat and follow with infusion 5 to 15 mcg per minute.

options.rationale: Refractory anaphylaxis after two IM adrenaline doses requires an IV adrenaline infusion; in beta-blocker refractoriness, IV glucagon 1 to 5 mg bolus bypasses the beta-receptor block via cAMP. (Source: ANZAAG Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
IM boluses have a ceiling and delayed absorption in shock; IV infusion is required in refractory anaphylaxis with sustained hypotension after two IM doses. (Source: ANZAAG Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

Adrenaline is the first line vasoactive drug in anaphylaxis (alpha and beta effects, mast cell stabilisation); noradrenaline is a second line adjunct only if adrenaline is insufficient. (Source: ANZAAG Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
Corticosteroids and antihistamines are adjunctive and do not treat acute shock; withholding IV adrenaline infusion in refractory anaphylaxis is unsafe. (Source: ANZAAG Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
Dopamine is not first line in anaphylaxis; worsening stridor with sustained shock mandates prompt airway management, not delay. (Source: ANZAAG Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

explanation.summary: PE diagnostic strategy uses Wells score to stratify patients into PE-unlikely (Wells <=4) or PE-likely (Wells >4). In PE-unlikely, D-dimer (age-adjusted for over 50 using age x 10 in micrograms/L) rules out PE when below cut-off. In PE-likely, D-dimer is bypassed and imaging is performed regardless. CT pulmonary angiography is first-line unless contrast contraindicated (severe renal impairment eGFR <30, contrast allergy, pregnancy) when V/Q scan is preferred. Doppler of legs supports diagnosis if positive but does not exclude PE if negative.
key_points: Wells >4 = PE-likely: image regardless of D-dimer
Wells <=4 plus age-adjusted D-dimer below cut-off rules out PE
CTPA first-line if renal function adequate
V/Q scan when CTPA contraindicated
explanation.pearls: Age-adjusted D-dimer cut-off (age x 10 mcg/L) reduces false positives in >50s from around 40 to 25 percent without affecting negative predictive value; adopted in AU and European guidelines but the standard 500 mcg/L cut-off remains used in some centres.

options.rationale: Two-level Wells >4 places the patient in the PE-likely group where CTPA is indicated regardless of D-dimer; her Wells of 4.5 with normal renal function makes CTPA the imaging of choice. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society ANZ 2021)

D-dimer strategies (standard or age-adjusted) are only validated in PE-unlikely groups (Wells <=4); a moderate to high probability Wells score requires imaging regardless of D-dimer. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society ANZ 2021)

With a Wells score of 4.5 (PE likely, >4) the age-adjusted D-dimer strategy is NOT applicable; D-dimer testing is reserved for Wells <=4 (PE unlikely); imaging is required regardless of D-dimer in Wells >4. However Wells 4.5 puts patient in the PE-likely group so CTPA is warranted. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society ANZ 2021)

V/Q scan is an alternative when CTPA is contraindicated (contrast allergy, severe renal impairment, pregnancy); with eGFR 62 CTPA is safer and faster for interpretation. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society ANZ 2021)

Doppler ultrasound of legs is used to detect DVT when PE is suspected and imaging is not immediately available; a positive DVT plus clinical PE suspicion treats as PE, but with eGFR 62 CTPA is not contraindicated and is the definitive investigation. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society ANZ 2021)

explanation.summary: Severe hyperkalaemia (>=6.5 mmol/L or ECG changes) is a medical emergency treated in three parallel steps: membrane stabilisation with IV calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent (or calcium chloride 5-10 mL of 10 percent via central line) repeated as needed; potassium shift with insulin-dextrose (10 units actrapid with 50 mL of 50 percent glucose) and nebulised salbutamol 10-20 mg; and definitive removal with haemodialysis in ESRD, or resonium and diuretics in preserved renal function. Cease contributing drugs (ACE inhibitor, ARB, spironolactone, NSAID). Continuous cardiac monitoring is essential.
key_points: IV calcium first for ECG changes (membrane stabilisation)
Insulin-dextrose plus salbutamol for shift
Haemodialysis for definitive removal in ESRD
Cease ACEI, ARB, spironolactone, NSAID
explanation.pearls: Calcium gluconate onset is 1-3 minutes with duration 30-60 minutes; repeat if ECG unchanged 5 minutes after first dose; calcium chloride has three times the elemental calcium of calcium gluconate but requires central access due to sclerosant risk.

sources.label: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for CKD

options.rationale: The ECG changes confirm the biochemical hyperkalaemia; awaiting repeat testing risks cardiac arrest during the wait. (Source: eTG Complete Acute Hyperkalaemia)

Resonium is a slow-acting cation exchange resin with modest effect and does not address life-threatening ECG changes; membrane stabilisation with calcium is the immediate step. (Source: eTG Complete Acute Hyperkalaemia)

Salbutamol lowers potassium modestly by around 0.5-1.0 mmol/L but does not stabilise the myocardium; calcium is the immediate priority in ECG changes of this severity. (Source: eTG Complete Acute Hyperkalaemia)

Bicarbonate has role in severe metabolic acidosis but does not stabilise the myocardium acutely; calcium precedes bicarbonate and shift strategies in acute hyperkalaemia with ECG changes. (Source: eTG Complete Acute Hyperkalaemia)

Hyperkalaemia with peaked T waves, PR prolongation, and QRS widening requires immediate IV calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent for membrane stabilisation, then insulin-dextrose (10 units actrapid with 50 mL of 50 percent glucose) for shift, and dialysis for definitive removal in this ESRD patient. (Source: eTG Complete Acute Hyperkalaemia)

explanation.summary: Acute severe asthma requires stepwise escalation. Initial therapy is oxygen (target SpO2 93-95 percent), continuous or back to back salbutamol nebuliser plus ipratropium, and oral prednisolone 50 mg (or IV hydrocortisone if not tolerating oral). If no response, escalate to IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 min, then consider IV aminophylline or salbutamol infusion with critical care admission. A normal pCO2 in a tachypnoeic patient is a sign of impending respiratory failure and mandates critical care review. Intubation carries high mortality in asthma and is a last resort, ideally with senior anaesthetic input.
key_points: Rising or normal pCO2 in tachypnoea signals exhaustion
IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 min is first-line escalation
Critical care admission for severe unresponsive asthma
Intubation last resort, high mortality
explanation.pearls: Ventilating an asthmatic requires permissive hypercapnia strategy with low tidal volumes (5-6 mL/kg IBW), low respiratory rate (8-10/min), and long expiratory time (I:E 1:4 or greater) to avoid dynamic hyperinflation and pneumothorax.

options.rationale: After adequate nebulised bronchodilator and oral steroid with no improvement (PEF 40 percent, exhausting pattern with a normal pCO2), escalation to IV magnesium and IV aminophylline consideration plus critical care review is indicated, not merely repeating oral steroid. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)

Severe asthma exacerbation not responding to standard therapy with signs of exhaustion (normal pCO2 in tachypnoea is pre-arrest) requires IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 min, critical care admission, and preparation for possible ventilation. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)

NIV for asthma is limited evidence and not first-line escalation; IV magnesium and consideration of aminophylline precede a decision to intubate rather than NIV in severe asthma. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)

IV hydrocortisone is a reasonable step but oral prednisolone has already been given and there is no benefit from IV over oral if oral is tolerated; the priority is IV magnesium and critical care escalation given exhaustion. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)

Adrenaline is reserved for anaphylaxis or peri-arrest asthma; IV magnesium is first-line escalation in severe asthma unresponsive to inhaled bronchodilators and oral steroid. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)

explanation.summary: DOAC reversal is agent-specific. Dabigatran (direct thrombin inhibitor) is reversed with idarucizumab 5 g (two 2.5 g doses). Apixaban and rivaroxaban (factor Xa inhibitors) are reversed with andexanet alfa where available, or 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate 50 units/kg as alternative. Activated charcoal 50 g reduces absorption if given within 2 hours of ingestion. Standard supportive measures include IV access, fluid and packed cell resuscitation, cessation of the DOAC, treatment of the source (endoscopy for upper GI, embolisation for GI), and PPI infusion for peptic ulcer bleeding.
key_points: Apixaban / rivaroxaban: andexanet or 4-factor PCC
Dabigatran: idarucizumab 5 g
Activated charcoal within 2 hours of ingestion
FFP and vitamin K have no role in DOAC reversal
explanation.pearls: The apixaban half-life is around 12 hours; 4-factor PCC (Prothrombinex-VF) contains factors II, VII, IX, X and rapidly restores thrombin generation but does not remove the drug from plasma; andexanet acts as a decoy Xa binding the drug.

options.rationale: FFP does not reverse DOACs (no factor deficiency to replace); direct-acting agents are reversed with specific reversal agents or prothrombin complex concentrate. (Source: THANZ 2019 DOAC Reversal)

Apixaban is a factor Xa inhibitor; specific reversal is andexanet alfa (limited AU availability); alternative is 4-factor PCC 50 units/kg; activated charcoal within 2 hours of ingestion reduces further absorption. (Source: THANZ 2019 DOAC Reversal)
Vitamin K reverses warfarin, not DOACs; apixaban is not a vitamin K antagonist and vitamin K has no effect on it. (Source: THANZ 2019 DOAC Reversal)

Idarucizumab is the monoclonal antibody Fab fragment that reverses dabigatran (a direct thrombin inhibitor); it has no activity against apixaban (factor Xa inhibitor). (Source: THANZ 2019 DOAC Reversal)

Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic and adjunct in bleeding but does not reverse the anticoagulant effect of DOACs; specific reversal (andexanet or 4-factor PCC) is required. (Source: THANZ 2019 DOAC Reversal)

explanation.summary: Status epilepticus management is time-critical. First-line: IV benzodiazepine (midazolam 10 mg IM or IV, lorazepam 4 mg IV, diazepam 10 mg IV; repeat once at 5-10 minutes). Second-line at 20-30 minutes: IV levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (max 4500 mg), sodium valproate 40 mg/kg (max 3000 mg), or phenytoin 20 mg/kg. ESETT trial (2019) showed all three equivalent (around 45 percent seizure termination); levetiracetam is preferred for its safety. Third-line (refractory status) at 40-60 minutes: continuous IV midazolam or propofol infusion with intubation and EEG monitoring. Non-convulsive status warrants EEG-guided titration.
key_points: First-line: benzodiazepine, repeat once
Second-line: levetiracetam, valproate, or phenytoin
Refractory (third-line): midazolam or propofol infusion, intubate
Address causes: hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, drug toxicity
explanation.pearls: ESETT (Established Status Epilepticus Treatment Trial, 2019 NEJM) compared fosphenytoin, valproate, and levetiracetam as second-line: no difference in seizure termination (around 45-47 percent), and no difference in adverse events; choice is guided by patient factors and centre preference.

options.rationale: Thiopental is used in refractory status epilepticus after failed second-line agent; jumping to induction agent skips the effective second-line step and commits to intubation prematurely. (Source: eTG Complete Neurology)

Phenytoin is effective but has cardiac risks (arrhythmia, hypotension) requiring slow infusion and monitoring, and interacts with many drugs; levetiracetam is generally preferred first-choice second-line in AU practice for its safety. (Source: eTG Complete Neurology)

Midazolam infusion is third-line (refractory status) after failed second-line agent; escalating to infusion without trying a second-line non-benzodiazepine agent commits to intubation prematurely. (Source: eTG Complete Neurology)

ESETT trial (2019) showed levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, valproate 40 mg/kg, and fosphenytoin equivalent in second-line status; levetiracetam is preferred in most AU centres for its safety profile, no need for cardiac monitoring beyond basic, and lack of interactions. (Source: eTG Complete Neurology)

Magnesium is second-line specifically for eclamptic seizures; in status epilepticus without pregnancy, levetiracetam, valproate, or phenytoin are the evidence-based second-line options. (Source: eTG Complete Neurology)

explanation.summary: Adult DKA management follows fluid, potassium, insulin, and ongoing monitoring stages. First fluid is 0.9 percent saline 1 L over 30 min to restore intravascular volume; ADS and increasing evidence favour balanced crystalloid (Hartmann's or Plasmalyte) after the first bolus to reduce hyperchloraemic acidosis, which prolongs anion gap closure. Potassium must be measured before insulin; <3.5 mandates supplementation and delaying insulin; 3.5-5.5 add 20-40 mmol/L KCl to fluids; >5.5 no supplementation until falls. Insulin at 0.1 units/kg/hour reduces ketones by around 0.5 mmol/L/hour. Dextrose added when glucose falls below 14 mmol/L. Bicarbonate reserved for pH <6.9 with cardiovascular compromise; even then evidence is limited.
key_points: First bolus 0.9 percent saline, then consider balanced crystalloid
Delay insulin until potassium >=3.5
Add dextrose when glucose <14
Bicarbonate not routine, even at low pH
explanation.pearls: The PLUS trial (2022 NEJM) in critically ill adults showed no mortality difference between saline and Plasmalyte, but DKA-specific data (SCOPE-DKA, SALT-ED subgroup) suggest balanced fluids may reduce hyperchloraemic acidosis and speed anion gap closure without safety signal.

options.rationale: Potassium <3.5 mandates supplementation and delaying insulin until potassium 3.5 or higher; balanced crystalloid (Hartmann's) is preferred to reduce hyperchloraemic acidosis burden of ongoing 0.9 percent saline, particularly with early creatinine rise. (Source: ADS Adult DKA Guideline)

AU DKA protocols delay insulin until potassium is 3.5 or higher to avoid life-threatening hypokalaemia; potassium replacement and continued fluid resuscitation precede insulin in this case. (Source: ADS Adult DKA Guideline)
Insulin should be delayed until potassium 3.5+; 10 mmol/L is inadequate replacement for K 3.4 with insulin about to run; higher potassium content and delay insulin. (Source: ADS Adult DKA Guideline)

Bicarbonate is not recommended in DKA at pH >7.0 and has limited role even at pH <6.9 (worsens hypokalaemia, delays ketone clearance); resuscitation with balanced crystalloid and potassium correction is standard. (Source: ADS Adult DKA Guideline)

Dextrose is added when glucose falls below 14 mmol/L to maintain insulin infusion while resolving ketosis; at glucose 32 mmol/L balanced crystalloid without dextrose is appropriate. (Source: ADS Adult DKA Guideline)

explanation.summary: Immune checkpoint inhibitor endocrinopathies include hypothyroidism (nivolumab), hypophysitis with secondary AI (ipilimumab, especially combination therapy), and less often type 1 diabetes. Adrenal crisis in this setting is characterised by hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, hypotension, low cortisol with inappropriately normal or low ACTH (secondary), and often coexisting central hypothyroidism. Treatment is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 100 mg 6 hourly (mineralocorticoid activity at these doses is adequate); IV volume resuscitation with dextrose-containing crystalloid; correct precipitants; withhold checkpoint inhibitor pending endocrine review. Coexisting central hypothyroidism requires cortisol replacement first, then levothyroxine.
key_points: Ipilimumab combination hypophysitis: secondary AI
IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 6 hourly
Never give levothyroxine before cortisol in coexisting AI
Withhold checkpoint inhibitor pending review
explanation.pearls: Baseline morning cortisol >500 nmol/L rules out AI; <100 nmol/L makes it likely; 100-500 nmol/L needs Synacthen (250 mcg tetracosactide) testing with 30 and 60 minute cortisol, though in secondary AI the adrenal has not yet atrophied so response can be preserved acutely.

sources.label: ESMO Immune Related Adverse Events Guidelines

options.rationale: Combined hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, postural collapse, low cortisol with normal potassium and low ACTH (secondary AI from ipilimumab-induced hypophysitis) is adrenal crisis; treatment is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 6 hourly and IV dextrose in saline resuscitation; also need to consider levothyroxine after cortisol has been replaced (never before, to avoid precipitating crisis). (Source: RCH-based eTG Adrenal Crisis and Endocrine Society Immune Endocrinopathy Guidelines)

Giving levothyroxine before cortisol replacement in coexisting secondary AI precipitates adrenal crisis by increasing metabolic demand for cortisol; steroid must be given first. (Source: eTG Complete Endocrinology)

Hypertonic saline is reserved for seizures or symptomatic severe hyponatraemia; adrenal-crisis hyponatraemia corrects with volume resuscitation plus cortisol replacement, and giving hypertonic without cortisol risks osmotic demyelination and delays treatment. (Source: eTG Complete Endocrinology)
Dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity and does not allow subsequent Synacthen testing; hydrocortisone is the correct steroid for adrenal crisis. (Source: eTG Complete Endocrinology)
Cessation of the offending agent is required but does not treat the acute crisis; IV hydrocortisone is life-saving and must not be delayed. (Source: eTG Complete Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Mixed HHS with euglycaemic DKA (or overt DKA) features requires an HHS-predominant strategy when osmolality and corrected sodium are the driving issues. Fluid replacement is slower than DKA to avoid cerebral oedema and osmotic demyelination: aim sodium reduction <=10 mmol/L per 24 hours and osmolality reduction <=3 mmol/kg per hour. Use 0.9 percent saline first, switching to 0.45 percent saline when corrected sodium rises further despite therapy. Insulin at 0.05 units/kg/hour (lower than standard DKA) sufficient because SGLT2-inhibitor-associated euglycaemic DKA has slower ketone clearance and increased ketone production risk. Empagliflozin ceased. VBG and osmolality every 2-4 hours guide titration.
key_points: HHS-predominant: slower rehydration than DKA
Sodium reduction <=10 mmol/L per 24 h
Low-dose insulin 0.05 units/kg/h
Cease SGLT2 inhibitor
explanation.pearls: Corrected sodium formula: measured sodium + 0.3 x (glucose - 5.5) mmol/L (Katz correction) or the older 2.4 factor per 5.5 mmol/L glucose above 5.5; monitor real (not measured) sodium as glucose falls, because it will rise; anticipate potassium falling as insulin acts.

options.rationale: Dextrose is added when glucose falls below 14 mmol/L; starting with dextrose at glucose 44 mmol/L is inappropriate and does not correct volume deficit. (Source: ADS HHS Position Statement)

HHS-predominant with corrected sodium 160 requires slower fluid replacement over 24-48 hours (aim sodium reduction <=10 mmol/L per 24 hours) to avoid cerebral oedema; standard DKA-rate fluids risk osmotic demyelination and cerebral oedema. (Source: ADS HHS Position Statement)

0.45 percent saline as bolus can cause too-rapid sodium correction and cerebral oedema; first resuscitation uses 0.9 percent saline at controlled rate, switching to 0.45 percent later based on corrected sodium and osmolality changes. (Source: ADS HHS Position Statement)

Mixed HHS with SGLT2-inhibitor-associated euglycaemic DKA features requires slower fluid replacement in HHS-predominant picture (osmolality 348, sodium 152, corrected sodium 160) to avoid cerebral oedema, plus low-dose insulin at 0.05 units/kg/hour and delayed ketone clearance strategy; empagliflozin ceased. (Source: ADS HHS Position Statement)

Rapid fluid and insulin in HHS with high corrected sodium risks cerebral oedema; controlled rehydration and low-dose insulin are safer; a bolus of insulin is not recommended in HHS. (Source: ADS HHS Position Statement)

explanation.summary: Suspected bacterial meningitis in an adult requires antibiotic administration within one hour of presentation - imaging and lumbar puncture must not delay this. Empirical AU regimen is IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly plus benzylpenicillin 2.4 g 4-hourly (adds Listeria cover for over 50 or immunocompromised; vancomycin substitutes if pneumococcal resistance is likely). IV dexamethasone 10 mg 6-hourly for 4 days is given with or before the first antibiotic to reduce mortality and neurological sequelae in pneumococcal meningitis. LP is deferred if reduced GCS, focal neurology, seizure, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, or haemodynamic instability - CT first, then LP once safe. Public health notification for meningococcal disease is immediate; household contacts require rifampicin or ciprofloxacin prophylaxis.
key_points: Antibiotics within 1 hour of presentation; do not delay for imaging or LP
IV ceftriaxone 2 g + benzylpenicillin 2.4 g (add vancomycin if resistance concern)
IV dexamethasone 10 mg with or before the first antibiotic dose
LP deferred if reduced GCS, focal deficit, seizure, coagulopathy
Public health notification + contact prophylaxis for meningococcal
explanation.pearls: In an unwell patient in whom pneumococcal resistance is a concern (recent travel, prior beta-lactam use, immunocompromised), add IV vancomycin 25-30 mg/kg loading; the AMR rate for penicillin-resistant pneumococcus in Australia remains low but rising in specific populations.

options.rationale: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in the presence of reduced GCS, focal neurological deficit, seizure, coagulopathy or haemodynamic instability without prior imaging, and antibiotics must not be delayed by LP or imaging. Every hour of delay in bacterial meningitis increases mortality. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - meningitis)

Airway protection may be needed if GCS falls further, but empirical antibiotics and dexamethasone must not be delayed. Mannitol is used for confirmed raised ICP with imaging or clinical evidence of impending herniation, not empirically. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - meningitis)

Oral antibiotics for bacterial meningitis are inadequate. Admission to the medical ward without ICU-level care in a shocked, seizing patient with meningism and purpura is negligent. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - meningitis)

Purpuric rash and rapid onset with meningism points to bacterial meningitis (meningococcal, pneumococcal). Aciclovir may be added if HSV encephalitis is a differential but does not replace bacterial cover. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - meningitis)

In suspected bacterial meningitis in adults the eTG-recommended empirical regimen is IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly plus benzylpenicillin 2.4 g 4-hourly (to cover Listeria in >50 years or immunocompromised) with IV dexamethasone 10 mg 6-hourly for 4 days ideally given before or with the first antibiotic dose (reduces pneumococcal mortality and neurological sequelae). Ceftriaxone plus vancomycin is used if pneumococcal resistance is a concern. LP is deferred until GCS improves and coagulopathy is corrected. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - meningitis)

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection is a surgical emergency with mortality 20-50 percent. Clinical features include pain out of proportion, systemic sepsis disproportionate to skin findings, dusky skin, bullae, crepitus, rapid extension, and shock. LRINEC score >=6 is suggestive (>=8 strongly suggestive) but negative LRINEC does not exclude. Empirical antibiotics: broad-spectrum beta-lactam (piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem) plus clindamycin (anti-toxin, Eagle effect against group A strep) plus vancomycin (MRSA). Aggressive fluid resuscitation.
key_points: Pain out of proportion + systemic sepsis + dusky skin/bullae = surgical emergency
LRINEC >=6 suggestive, >=8 strongly suggestive; negative does not exclude
Meropenem + clindamycin + vancomycin empirical
Emergency operative debridement within 6 hours
HBO and IVIG adjunctive; return to theatre in 24 hours for reassessment
explanation.pearls: Clindamycin adds anti-exotoxin effect against group A streptococcus and Staphylococcus aureus (Eagle effect - beta-lactam efficacy falls at high bacterial burden), and is included even where the pathogen is likely a mixed polymicrobial synergistic infection.

sources.label: eTG Complete Antibiotic - skin and soft tissue

options.rationale: This is necrotising fasciitis (pain out of proportion, dusky skin, bullae, systemic sepsis, LRINEC 10, rising creatinine). Continuing narrow-spectrum monotherapy without surgical review is fatal. Time to debridement is the primary determinant of mortality. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic - skin and soft tissue

options.rationale: Necrotising soft tissue infection is a surgical emergency. AU empirical antibiotic cover is IV meropenem (Gram-negative and anaerobe cover) plus IV clindamycin (anti-toxin, streptococcal Eagle effect) plus IV vancomycin (MRSA cover). Aggressive fluid resuscitation and immediate operative debridement within 6 hours reduce mortality from over 50 percent toward 20 percent. Every hour of delay increases mortality. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic - skin and soft tissue

options.rationale: MRI can be useful when the diagnosis is uncertain but must never delay operative debridement in a septic patient with clear clinical features of nec fasc. Diagnosis is primarily clinical; surgery is diagnostic and therapeutic. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic - skin and soft tissue

options.rationale: HBO is an adjunctive therapy after adequate surgical debridement and antibiotic control, not a substitute or antecedent. Time to surgical debridement is the primary mortality determinant. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic - skin and soft tissue

options.rationale: Adding metronidazole to flucloxacillin does not provide adequate anti-toxin or MRSA cover, and ward-level observation without surgical debridement is inappropriate for necrotising fasciitis. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic - skin and soft tissue

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis in known primary adrenal insufficiency is treated with IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 50 mg every 6 hours (or 200 mg/24 hr infusion), aggressive 0.9 percent saline fluid resuscitation, glucose correction, and search for the precipitant (infection is commonest). Hydrocortisone at stress dose has sufficient mineralocorticoid activity that fludrocortisone can be deferred until oral intake resumes. Sick-day rules for Addisonians: double the oral hydrocortisone dose for febrile illness or moderate physiological stress; hydrocortisone 100 mg IM or IV for vomiting/inability to take oral, then present to hospital. All patients should carry a MedicAlert, wear the bracelet, and have hydrocortisone 100 mg IM emergency ampoule at home. Prevention through education reduces mortality.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 50 mg Q6H (or 200 mg/24 h infusion)
1 L 0.9% saline stat + glucose correction
Search for precipitant (infection most common)
Sick-day rules: double oral dose; IM hydrocortisone 100 mg if unable to tolerate oral
Patient should have MedicAlert + home IM ampoule + education
explanation.pearls: Cortisone acetate 100 mg IM is the alternative if hydrocortisone unavailable; the peak cortisol level from IM cortisone is lower and slower than IM hydrocortisone but sufficient to bridge to hospital care - carry this in remote-work or extended-travel patients.

sources.label: Endocrine Society AI clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: The diagnosis is already established (known Addison's on stable replacement); short synacthen test is not needed. Hydrocortisone is the correct replacement because it has mineralocorticoid activity at stress dose; dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity and does not correct the hyponatraemia/hyperkalaemia. (Source: Endocrine Society AI clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society AI clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Adrenal crisis in a known Addisonian is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat followed by 50 mg every 6 hours (or a 200 mg/24 hour infusion) with aggressive fluid resuscitation with 0.9 percent saline (1 L over 30 minutes then reassess) and correction of hypoglycaemia. Hydrocortisone provides sufficient mineralocorticoid effect at stress dose so fludrocortisone is deferred until oral intake resumes. Investigate the precipitant. Diagnostic cortisol and ACTH are drawn before the first hydrocortisone dose if not already established. (Source: Endocrine Society AI clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society AI clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Fludrocortisone has no parenteral form and takes days to act. Withholding hydrocortisone in a shocked Addisonian is life-threatening. (Source: Endocrine Society AI clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society AI clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: IV hydrocortisone is required in adrenal crisis - oral or NG absorption in a vomiting shocked patient is unreliable. Speed of onset with IV is critical to reversing shock. (Source: Endocrine Society AI clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society AI clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Vasopressors are ineffective in adrenal crisis without glucocorticoid replacement because vascular smooth muscle is refractory to catecholamines in cortisol deficiency. Hydrocortisone must precede or accompany any vasopressor. (Source: Endocrine Society AI clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society AI clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Acute pyelonephritis in adults presents with fever, flank pain, and lower urinary tract symptoms. Hospital admission is warranted for systemic sepsis, dehydration, inability to tolerate oral, pregnancy, or complicated urinary tract abnormality. Empirical therapy per eTG: IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg once daily plus IV amoxicillin 2 g six-hourly, then switch to oral guided by susceptibility once afebrile and tolerating oral (typical agents cefalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, ciprofloxacin, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole). Total duration 10-14 days for uncomplicated adult pyelonephritis. Ceftriaxone 1 g daily is the alternative if aminoglycoside contraindicated (renal impairment, elderly, prolonged duration). Ultrasound is warranted if response is slow, obstruction is suspected, or the patient is diabetic.
key_points: First-line: IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg + IV amoxicillin (eTG)
Ceftriaxone if aminoglycoside contraindicated
Total duration 10-14 days
Switch oral once afebrile 24-48 h, tolerating oral, susceptibility known
Ultrasound if slow response, obstruction suspected, or diabetic
explanation.pearls: In an admitted pyelonephritis patient with slow response after 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics, image urgently for obstruction, emphysematous pyelonephritis (a diabetes emergency requiring urgent urology/decompression), or perinephric abscess.

sources.label: eTG Complete Antibiotic - urinary tract infection

options.rationale: Broad-spectrum agents like piperacillin-tazobactam are reserved for severe sepsis, prior ESBL colonisation, healthcare-associated infection, or after culture-directed switch. Empirical use in a stable community-acquired pyelonephritis is unnecessary and drives resistance. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - urinary tract infection)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic - urinary tract infection

options.rationale: Fluoroquinolones are reserved for gram-negative resistance patterns and specific patient factors due to AU stewardship and tendonopathy/QT concerns; they are not first-line empirical treatment for pyelonephritis. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - urinary tract infection)

options.rationale: Systemic sepsis features (fever, tachycardia, raised lactate, high WCC and CRP) warrant IV therapy and admission. Oral therapy is inadequate for hospital-admitted acute pyelonephritis. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - urinary tract infection)

options.rationale: eTG recommends IV gentamicin (5 mg/kg once-daily dosing, avoid if renal impairment or age >70 or long duration) plus IV amoxicillin as empirical therapy for adult non-pregnant acute pyelonephritis in a haemodynamically stable admitted patient. Total course 10-14 days. Switch to oral once afebrile 24-48 hours, tolerating oral, guided by susceptibility (cefalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, ciprofloxacin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole per sensitivities). (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: Preoperative preparation of phaeochromocytoma is critical to prevent intraoperative catecholamine-triggered hypertensive crisis and postoperative refractory hypotension. Alpha-blockade (phenoxybenzamine 10-20 mg twice daily titrated up, or doxazosin 4-16 mg daily as the AU preferred option in many centres) is initiated at least 10-14 days before surgery, with target orthostatic hypotension, mild nasal congestion, and BP <130/80 seated with SBP >90 standing. Liberal salt and fluid intake reverses catecholamine-induced volume contraction (usually 5 g salt/day plus 2-3 L fluid). Beta-blockade (propranolol, atenolol) is added ONLY after alpha-blockade is established, to control catecholamine-induced tachycardia; beta-before-alpha causes hypertensive crisis by unopposed alpha stimulation. Calcium channel blockers or metyrosine may be adjuncts. Intraoperative hypotension after tumour removal is managed with fluids and vasopressors.
key_points: Alpha-blockade at least 10-14 days before surgery
Phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin (AU preferred selective alpha-1)
Beta-blockade added AFTER alpha-blockade is established
Liberal salt and fluid intake (5 g NaCl + 2-3 L fluid) - reverses catecholamine volume contraction
Beta-first causes hypertensive crisis (unopposed alpha)
explanation.pearls: Metyrosine (tyrosine hydroxylase inhibitor) blocks catecholamine synthesis and is added for particularly biochemically active tumours or before surgery for metastatic disease when receptor blockade alone is insufficient - specialist endocrine referral required.

options.rationale: Preoperative preparation for phaeochromocytoma requires at least 10-14 days of alpha-blockade before surgery. Phenoxybenzamine (non-competitive, irreversible) is traditional; doxazosin (selective alpha-1) is an alternative and widely used in Australia. Beta-blockade is ADDED after alpha-blockade is established (target orthostatic hypotension, mild nasal congestion) to avoid unopposed alpha-agonism which precipitates hypertensive crisis. Liberal salt and fluid intake reverses catecholamine-induced volume contraction. (Source: Endocrine Society phaeochromocytoma guideline)

Beta-blockade before alpha-blockade precipitates severe hypertensive crisis by unopposed alpha stimulation (loss of beta-2 mediated vasodilation). This is a fatal sequencing error. Alpha always precedes beta. (Source: Endocrine Society phaeochromocytoma guideline)

Calcium channel blockers are second-line adjuncts to alpha-blockade, not substitutes. Deferring alpha-blockade until day-before surgery does not allow time to establish volume expansion and receptor blockade, and intraoperative haemodynamic swings become extreme and dangerous. (Source: Endocrine Society phaeochromocytoma guideline)

ACE inhibitors are not the primary agents for phaeochromocytoma-related hypertension. Salt restriction worsens intravascular volume contraction. This management strategy is inadequate and dangerous. (Source: Endocrine Society phaeochromocytoma guideline)

Labetalol has beta blockade activity greater than alpha (roughly 7:1 ratio when oral), so it delivers de facto beta-first blockade and is not an accepted preoperative regimen for phaeochromocytoma. Sequential alpha-then-beta with dedicated agents is the standard. (Source: Endocrine Society phaeochromocytoma guideline)

explanation.summary: Myasthenic crisis is bulbar and/or respiratory failure requiring intensive care. Common precipitants: infection, aspiration, non-compliance, medications (macrolides, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, magnesium, beta-blockers, high-dose IV corticosteroid). Assess respiratory function with vital capacity and NIP - VC <20 mL/kg (about 1 L in a 60 kg patient) or NIP less negative than -30 cmH2O warrants preparation for intubation. IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days and plasmapheresis (5-7 sessions) are equally effective; IVIG is often first-line in AU practice due to availability. Continue steroid to prevent adrenal crisis; pyridostigmine may be reduced. Immunomodulation with mycophenolate, azathioprine, or rituximab is planned for the outpatient long term. Precipitant removal (drug, infection treatment) is essential.
key_points: Crisis = respiratory/bulbar failure needing ICU
VC <20 mL/kg or NIP > -30 = prepare to intubate
IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days ~ plasmapheresis; IVIG usually AU first-line
Remove precipitant (macrolides, aminoglycosides, magnesium)
Continue steroid; pyridostigmine may be reduced in crisis
explanation.pearls: In seronegative myasthenia gravis (no anti-AChR antibody) check for anti-MuSK antibodies which are more common in women and often more bulbar-predominant with less pyridostigmine response - rituximab is particularly effective for MuSK-positive disease.

options.rationale: Myasthenic crisis is defined by respiratory or bulbar failure requiring intensive care admission and often ventilatory support. Vital capacity below 20 mL/kg (about 1.4 L in a 70 kg patient) or NIP less negative than -30 cmH2O warrants preparation for intubation. IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days is equivalent to plasmapheresis in efficacy (large trials show non-inferiority) but IVIG is more available, does not require specialised access, and is often the first-line AU choice. Removing the precipitant (azithromycin worsens myasthenia via presynaptic effect) is critical. Continue steroids because sudden withdrawal precipitates crisis. Pyridostigmine may need dose adjustment. (Source: RACP myasthenia gravis)

Escalating pyridostigmine in crisis risks cholinergic crisis (indistinguishable from myasthenic crisis except by edrophonium test) and increases secretions worsening respiratory function. In severe crisis pyridostigmine is often reduced or withheld. (Source: RACP myasthenia gravis)

High-dose steroids can transiently WORSEN myasthenic weakness before improvement (10-day worsening window). In active respiratory failure a rapid-acting immunotherapy (IVIG or plasmapheresis) is needed, not pulse steroid alone. (Source: RACP myasthenia gravis)

Edrophonium (Tensilon) testing carries significant risks (bradycardia, bronchospasm) and is largely superseded. Diagnosis rests on clinical picture, medication review and serial vital capacity. (Source: RACP myasthenia gravis)

Neostigmine has a shorter half-life and greater muscarinic effects than pyridostigmine and does not address the underlying immune process. Switching cholinesterase inhibitors is not disease-modifying. (Source: RACP myasthenia gravis)

explanation.summary: Aortic dissection: Stanford A involves the ascending aorta (~60 percent, surgical emergency, untreated mortality 1-2 percent per hour); Stanford B is distal to the left subclavian only (~40 percent, medical management with impulse control unless complicated). Initial management is aggressive impulse control: IV beta-blockade first (labetalol, esmolol, metoprolol) to HR 60-80 and SBP 100-120, then IV vasodilator (GTN, nitroprusside) if further BP control needed. Beta-blockade must precede vasodilator to prevent reflex tachycardia. Analgesia and cardiothoracic surgical referral for Type A. For Type B, TEVAR is indicated for malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain or hypertension. Long-term BP control, aggressive risk factor reduction, and imaging surveillance are lifelong.
key_points: Type A = ascending aorta = surgical emergency (~2%/hr untreated mortality)
Type B = distal only = medical management unless complicated (TEVAR)
Impulse control: beta-blockade FIRST to HR 60-80, SBP 100-120
Vasodilator (GTN, nitroprusside) added AFTER beta-blockade if needed
Anticoagulation contraindicated; opioid analgesia; urgent cardiothoracic referral
explanation.pearls: In dissection with new aortic regurgitation murmur or pericardial effusion, do not perform pericardiocentesis unless in extremis - decompressing the tamponade removes the tamponade effect that is limiting further bleeding into the pericardium and precipitates death from exsanguination into the pericardial sac.

options.rationale: Type A dissection is a surgical emergency regardless of complications - ascending aorta involvement carries prohibitive medical-management mortality within hours. Delaying surgery for outpatient review is fatal. (Source: eTG Complete Cardiology)

Vasodilators alone (nitroprusside, GTN) cause reflex tachycardia which increases aortic wall shear stress (dP/dt) and worsens dissection propagation. Beta-blockade must precede any vasodilator therapy. (Source: eTG Complete Cardiology)

Heparin in acute aortic dissection worsens haemorrhage and is contraindicated. CT aortogram has confirmed dissection - PE is not the diagnosis and empirical anticoagulation is harmful. (Source: eTG Complete Cardiology)

This is Stanford Type A dissection (ascending aorta involved). It is a surgical emergency with mortality of 1-2 percent per hour without operative repair. Management: aggressive impulse control with IV beta-blockade to target HR 60-80 and SBP 100-120 (labetalol infusion, or esmolol; add IV GTN if further BP control needed after HR is controlled - never before), analgesia (IV morphine), and immediate cardiothoracic surgical referral. Type B (descending only) is managed medically unless malperfusion or rupture. (Source: eTG Complete Cardiology / RACS aortic dissection)

TEVAR is the definitive intervention for complicated Type B dissections (malperfusion, rupture, uncontrolled pain). Type A dissections require open surgical repair; endovascular stenting of the ascending aorta is not standard first-line. (Source: eTG Complete Cardiology)
